recommendations.text:
Decide the A350 Re-engine on the ExCo's own tests and on an explicit read of Boeing. Put a probability on S2 and reason it from the bulletin. Boeing gave no Re-engine date and said the market, the technology and Boeing were not yet ready, but its readiness work continues and Charleston has headroom.
- The item breaks even at 58%: it is worth about +0.33 at 25%, +0.18 at 40% and +0.08 at 50%.
- Even at 0% it is only +0.57, under the $1B test, which is smaller than in 2045, as Toepfer's discount predicted.
- If his gate or Wagner's readiness test fails it, the right answer is hold. The Board will not read that as a lost opportunity, and it would not accept an override to carry it.

Engine path. Rolls-Royce is the A350 incumbent, but it spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine and keeps UltraFan as technology, with no product launch. An UltraFan WB launched alongside a 2050 airframe would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. Boeing's own record finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 entry into service. Wagner should name the engine, its readiness and the fallback. The engine path is not a veto ground on its own, unless he fails the launch on production readiness and that failure is overridden.

The long view beyond the board's horizon. Pay measures nothing beyond about four years, so the Board supplies the long view. Research and technology for the generation after NGSA, and studies on the A350 family's future, stay funded inside the Board-approved R&D budget as staged studies, each below EUR 300m of committed spend until a Board gate. An NGSA derivative or an A220 variant comes to the Board as its own item if it crosses EUR 300m, and a launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority. None is presented as a launch in public. The Board's annual off-site should review the staged portfolio.

Public statement.
- Lead with the five pillars and with NGSA's fleet safety and durability.
- Give windows, not dates.
- If the A350 Re-engine is launched, give no window the engine cannot meet, and make no reference to Boeing.
- If it is held, say the A350 family, including the A350F, remains the focus, decided on Airbus's own technology and industrial clock, and commit to nothing either way.
- Never mention Delay Tactics.
The Board vets the final text.

tests.name: Robustness, plan level (teams.md Step 2): plans A and B
tests.threshold: The plan's ΔPV against Do Nothing is positive in the worst plausible Boeing column (S2: Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine)
tests.numbers: A: +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2. B: +23.94 in S1 and +22.92 in S2. Both are positive in both columns (ask 3). The worst plausible column is S2: the bulletin says Boeing's readiness work on the 787's next step continues and Charleston has headroom, and no engine-maturity point rules out a 2050 launch. A's worst column (+23.33) beats B's (+22.92). Holding gives up only $0.04B in S2, the cost of a lone 787 Re-engine entering service in 2055.

tests.name: Robustness, added move: plan B (my added-move gate; the company's A350 Re-engine launch test, profile section 6)
tests.threshold: The added move must be worth at least $1B over the same plan without it in the expected column and must not be negative in the 787 Re-engine column. A move that misses $1B and turns negative in a plausible column fails
tests.numbers: Item value against plan A: +0.57 in S1 (23.94 - 23.37), which is $0.43B short of $1B, and -0.41 in S2 (22.92 - 23.33), negative in the worst plausible column. It fails on both counts. +0.57 is its ceiling, at 0% for S2, so it fails in whichever column is expected. -0.41 is inside the Board's $2B loss line, so my gate fails, not the Board's loss line. Not a red line and not a pillars breach. Soft veto, binding: true (ask 2).

tests.name: Expected value and break-even: plan B (ask 3)
tests.threshold: Company launch test in expectation: at least $1B over Do Nothing at any plausible chance of S2
tests.numbers: The item is worth 0.57 x (1-p) - 0.41 x p = 0.57 - 0.98p. By p(S2): 0%: +0.57 (ceiling); 20%: +0.37; 25%: +0.33; 30%: +0.28; 35%: +0.23; 40%: +0.18; 45%: +0.13; 50%: +0.08. It breaks even at 0.57 / 0.98 = 58.2%. Plan EVs at Faury's 30%: A 0.7 x 23.37 + 0.3 x 23.33 = $23.36B; B 0.7 x 23.94 + 0.3 x 22.92 = $23.63B, a gap of $0.28B. Faury's figures are confirmed. No probability brings the item to $1B, so the answer does not rest on the read of Boeing.

tests.name: Option to wait: check of my 2045 estimate against the 2050 grid (ask 4)
tests.threshold: Information for the Board; the added-move gate applies unchanged
tests.numbers: 2045 grid: +0.89 / -0.50. My 2045 estimate for a like-for-like 2050 launch was 0.89 x 1.08^-5 = 0.89 x 0.681 = +0.61, or +0.70 on my reconstruction. The 2050 grid gives +0.57: $0.04B under the discount estimate and $0.13B under the reconstruction. So the five-year discount explains almost all of the decline in S1, and my reconstruction ran high. The downside shrank less than the upside: -0.50 discounted would be -0.34, but the grid gives -0.41. The S2 loss is 72% of the S1 gain (0.41 / 0.57), against 56% in 2045 (0.50 / 0.89), so break-even fell from 64.0% to 58.2%. The brief does not let me decompose the residual, and I do not invent it. For the Board: waiting bought no better case, only the same case, smaller and with a heavier relative downside. No option is left to wait for: 2050 is the last decision year, so holding now holds for the rest of the game, and any widebody future continues off the board as staged studies.

tests.name: Overlap and one launch per round (rule 6): plan B
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 Re-engine development overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more, and at most one new launch per round
tests.numbers: NGSA has been in service since 2037. The A350 Re-engine would develop over 2050-55, so the overlap is 0 years. It is one launch in the round. Not a red line. Plan A launches nothing.

tests.name: Fine exposure, second move and poaching (rules 4 and 5)

tests.numbers: delay_tactics is none on both plans and is the only value on the menu. No move has been ordered in this game, so nothing is exposed.

tests.name: Net cash, rating and shareholder returns, base case beside stress case (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Payout within 30-50%; buybacks sized after the year's programme cash; no equity raise; no dividend cut outside a crisis; state money upside only. Rating proxy: net cash at or above zero every year, and programme spend within one year's free cash flow
tests.numbers:
Method (proxy, inference, unchanged from my 2045 schedule). The board's operating profit stands in for EBIT Adjusted. Free cash flow = operating profit x 4,753 / 7,128 (0.667). Net income = operating profit x 5,221 / 7,128 (0.732). Stress: free cash flow flat at FY2025's $5.23B and net income at $5.74B, with no NGSA uplift. $1.10 per €. Opening net-cash proxy at end-2049 (plan A held in 2045): +$43.6B base and +$3.7B stress.

2050-54 flows.
- Base: operating profit $15.9B gives free cash flow of $10.6B and net income of $11.65B. A 30-50% payout is $3.49-5.82B.
- Stress: free cash flow $5.23B, net income $5.74B, payout $1.72-2.87B.
- Programme cash: A $0; B $1.0B a year.

Buyback room after programme cash and a 50% payout: base $4.78B (A) and $3.78B (B); stress $2.36B (A) and $1.36B (B). At a 40% payout, stress B has $1.93B. The €5bn three-year programme runs at about $1.83B a year and is fundable in every case except stress + B + a 50% payout. There it is trimmed by about $0.47B, or the payout moves toward 40%. The buyback is trimmed first, never the programme gate. The 18-month AGM authority caps holdings at 10% of issued capital; the share price is not in my record, so I cannot state that cap in dollars.

Net-cash proxy at a 50% payout with the full buyback each year: end-2054 base +$58.3B (A) and +$53.3B (B). Stress: A rises from +$4.2B in 2050 to +$6.3B; B falls from +$3.2B in 2050 to +$1.3B in 2054, positive every year.

Rating: S&P A+ stable and Moody's A1 stable. The agencies' thresholds are still not in my record. Headroom proxy: net cash at or above zero every year (both plans pass), and programme spend against the line (A 0%, B 19%). No equity raise and no dividend cut in either case. State money is upside only, and refundable advances and risk-sharing stay outside the case.

tests.name: Capex timing (tie-break)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: A and B are within $1B in both columns (0.57 in S1, 0.41 in S2). A starts no capex; B starts $1.0B a year in 2050. The tie-break favours A.

tests.name: Board items
tests.threshold: Every order above €300m is a Board item; within $1B, prefer fewer
tests.numbers: A: 0 Board items; all four orders are defaults. B: 1 Board item, a launch above €800m (about $0.88B) that needs a Qualified Majority. The tie-break favours A.

tests.name: Cancel discipline and last-year governance (ask 5)
tests.threshold: Cancel an A350 Re-engine only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B; never cancel NGSA. Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years
tests.numbers:
Not launched under my recommendation. The cancel condition cannot be reached. A 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 enters service in 2055 at the earliest, the same year as ours, so it can never enter service first, and no later round exists in which to order a cancel. A launch would be an unconditional commitment carried through 2055.

If B were launched (governance off the board):
- The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) runs an annual cash gate at $1.0B a year over 2050-54 and reports any year above it.
- Write-off schedule ($5B x years elapsed / 5): $1B after one year, $2B after two, $3B after three, $4B after four, and the full $5B by the 2055 entry into service.
- Any write-off appears in reported EBIT beside EBIT Adjusted and is never adjusted away.
NGSA is in service, so no cancel arises.

tests.name: Override arithmetic, for the record (ask 7)
tests.threshold: An override needs the plan to be at least $1B better than the best passing option (plan A) and to be recorded as a Board item; at most one per game
tests.numbers: B against A: +0.57 in S1 ($0.43B short of $1B) and -0.41 in S2 (behind A in the worst plausible column). It fails the team rule in both columns. It also fails the Board's override review: a Qualified Majority item that trails hold by $0.41B in S2. The override budget is unused: overrides are empty in the sealed orders for rounds 1-3. No override can carry B, and the CEO has none against the Board.

tests.name: Staged widebody case, CFO gates, closing record (option C)
tests.threshold: Gates recorded in 2035: rule 3; A350F and Spirit (Wagner); a widebody engine ready by entry into service (Wagner); the grid gate (at least $1B in the expected column, not negative in the 787 column); peak cash; Qualified Majority

- A350F and Spirit: Wagner's gate; on the record I hold, it rests on the game proxy only.
- Engine: Wagner's gate. The record shows an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 ready only in 2056.
- Grid gate: failed in 2045 (+0.89 / -0.50) and fails again now (+0.57 / -0.41).

- Qualified Majority: required.
On the cash side the case closes on my grid gate whatever Wagner reports.

tests.name: Studies outside the board (ask 8)
tests.threshold: Any commitment above €300m is a Board item; studies stay staged, each with its own cash line

tests.name: Five pillars and integrity of the other moves

Supply agreements resized to our own needs (1,060 a year from 2049), never held at the 2039 peak: an integrity safeguard against over-contracting. vetoes.plan: B. Plan A + A350 Re-engine launched 2050 (entry into service 2055)

The item is +0.57 in S1, $0.43B short of $1B even at 0% for S2, and -0.41 in S2, negative in the worst plausible column. Peak cash passes ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom). The team rule therefore allows no override, and the Board's override review would fail it too. Whether to override is the CEO's call, not mine to pre-clear, but the arithmetic does not reach it.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) A grid on which the A350 Re-engine is worth at least $1B over hold in the expected column and is not negative in the 787 Re-engine column. This brief cannot show that: +0.57 is the ceiling, at 0% for S2. (2) A Board decision. (3) No later round exists, so no new information can arrive on the board. (4) On returns, not the order: if free cash flow runs near FY2025's $5.2B with a 50% payout and the full €5bn buyback, the stress proxy with plan B falls to +$1.3B by 2054. I would trim the buyback first, never the programme gate. (5) A safety, quality, durability or supply flag from Wagner would only strengthen hold.
cfo.memo:
Board paper, 2050 (CFO), for the Audit Committee. The line is one year's free cash flow: €4,753m, about $5.2B [AX-0104].

Cash. Plan A carries no programme cash. Plan B spends $1.0B a year over 2050-54, entry into service 2055: no NGSA overlap, no strain, one launch, $4.2B under the line. Both pass. Cash is not the constraint.

Value. A: +23.37 / +23.33. B: +23.94 / +22.92. The launch alone is +0.57 in S1, $0.43B short of $1B, and -0.41 in S2, the worst plausible column. It fails my added-move gate on both counts: soft veto, binding. Its margin over plan A, the best passing option, is +0.57 / -0.41, so no override can carry it. Break-even is 58% for S2; at 30% it is worth +0.28. The answer does not rest on the read of Boeing.

Waiting. My 2045 estimate was +0.61; the grid gives +0.57. Waiting bought the same case, smaller, with a heavier relative downside (break-even down from 64%). No option remains: this is the last decision year and the cancel condition cannot be reached, so a launch would be a commitment without a gate.

Balance sheet (proxy). Net cash stays positive to 2054 in base and stress; payout within 30-50%; buybacks sized after programme cash. Agency thresholds are not in my record. No equity raise; state money upside only.

Recommendation: plan A. Engine code None, on Wagner's call.

Public line: disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

tests.name: Safety and quality on NGSA, the A320neo and the A350, both options. This is a safety and quality result, which neither the CEO nor the Board overrides.
tests.threshold: No safety or quality issue open on the record, and no order whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no safety, quality, durability or supply problem. The GM recorded no public events in 2045, and there is no inject. My record stops at the two end-2025 technical issues under root-cause investigation and the A320 quality reports [AX-0056, AX-0057], and nothing since then is on the board. So no issue is open on the record, but I have no line data to confirm that from. Where the record is silent, I say so.
- Plan A adds nothing to review.
- Plan B stands on the pillars only if its public window is one the engine can meet. The board books entry into service in 2055, but the only engine path is ready in 2056 (see the readiness test). 'Around the middle of the decade' would therefore overstate it.

tests.name: In-service durability of both NGSA engine families, the CFM ducted and the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine. This is a safety result.
tests.threshold: Any durability flag from an engine maker reaches the Board before the orders and is answered through supply and fleet action, never by re-timing NGSA. Nothing added may draw on the people, shops or supplier slots behind the durability work.
tests.numbers:
Both engines have been in service since 2036 and on NGSA since 2037, so 13-14 years.

Time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits: the brief gives no figure for either engine family, so the record is silent.
- CFM measures time on wing in cycles against the CFM56 yardstick and reports only on field data.
- P&W will report the fleet record.
- RR ranks safety first, then time on wing and full-life parts.
None of them publishes a number.

Flags: none on the record.
- CFM said any flag would reach the Board before the 2050 orders, with its fleet action. None has.
- CFM's hot-and-harsh remark is Ali's inference from the LEAP history, labelled 'not a flag'. I do not read it as a flag.
- P&W gives no dated recovery of its GTF AOG count and offers the Hot Section kit at shop visits. That concerns the A320neo GTF fleet, not NGSA, and the brief gives no count. I carry it as a watch item, not a flag.

What each plan would draw on:
- Plan A draws on nothing.
- Plan B is airframe work for a widebody team on our side. At the supplier, it would put a new Rolls-Royce widebody engine beside RR's Joint Venture fleet support and its Trent durability work (about GBP 1bn over four years). RR keeps the Trent durability money apart from the UltraFan money, but the record says nothing about its engineers or shops. I cannot fail B on that ground, and I cannot confirm the ring-fence at the supplier either.

tests.name: The NGSA line and the A320neo transition: the ramp shield. This is a ramp result, which neither the CEO nor the Board overrides.
tests.threshold: Nothing added draws on the people or supplier slots that carry the NGSA line or the A320neo transition. On this board the test passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.
tests.numbers:
Our narrowbody deliveries on the board:
- 1,260 at the 2039 peak (63% share);
- 1,140 in 2045 (57%);
- 1,060 from 2049 (53%), on the long-run 47/53 split.
Operating profit is $15.9B a year from 2049. The fall comes from share, not from a line or quality problem.

The board carries no monthly rate and does not split NGSA deliveries from A320neo deliveries. For the A320neo transition I can therefore report only that no problem is reported.

Plan A adds no load. Plan B draws on no narrowbody line if it is staffed from a named widebody team. This report goes to the safety review as one package with the durability record.

tests.name: Supply crunch. This is a supply result, which neither the CEO nor the Board overrides.
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency.
tests.numbers: No crunch, shortfall or inject is reported. Narrowbody engine shares in 2049 were CFM 56.8%, P&W 21.6% and RR 21.6%, a stable three-way split since 2037. Had a crunch been reported before the orders, B would fail outright and hold would stand.

tests.name: Joint Venture watch item and engine code. This is a recommendation, not a veto ground.
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker. Flag any supply watch item.
tests.numbers:
Code None is the only value on the menu. The fitted set (CFM, P&W and RR) stands, which gives three sources.

The Joint Venture position is unchanged:
- P&W and RR still ride on one engine, so a single Joint Venture problem would hit two of our three sources.
- Their shares have stayed equal: 21.6% each in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is consistent with Boeing's CFM-only fps gaining share, not with a delivery shortfall (inference).
- P&W's GTF fleet, its new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on its parts, shops and engineers.
- CFM is the backstop, held as flexibility within our resized needs, never as extra slots.

No shortfall is reported.

tests.name: Supply-agreement resizing and integrity limits (rules 4 and 5), for the ECSC review. This is a pillars result.
tests.threshold: Agreements resized to our own needs (1,140 aircraft in 2045, 1,060 from 2049) and never held at the 2039 peak of 1,260. Any agreement above EUR 300m comes to the Board. Hiring never targets rival teams. Delay Tactics none.
tests.numbers:
Supply: the resizing was ordered in 2045 and published as a more sovereign European supply chain sized to our own programmes. Our needs fall by about 16% from the peak (1,260 to 1,060 aircraft). The brief gives no outcome and no agreement values, so I cannot name any agreement that crosses EUR 300m. The ECSC must report each one (engines from all three makers, wing packages, titanium forgings, rare earths) and bring any above EUR 300m to the Board.

Hiring: open European recruitment, sized to NGSA in-service support, the A320neo transition and the staged studies, never aimed at rival teams.

Delay Tactics: none, the only value on the menu. The window closed in 2040, and no move was ordered in rounds 1 to 3. No supply or hiring lever is used to do what Delay Tactics would do.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption, plan B. This is a soft-veto ground.
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: 2035 at the earliest (company window 2033-35).
tests.numbers:
B passes on the game proxy only: 2050 is 15 years past the 2035 floor.

My record stops at end-2025:
- the A350F in its industrial phase, with its first two prototypes in final assembly [AX-0082];
- the Spirit A350 packages acquired [AX-0060].
The brief gives no A350F or Spirit status for any later year. Widebody share has been flat at 41.2%, 70 aircraft a year, since 2026.

I cannot confirm either gate from line data, so the Board's condition that I confirm them from line data is not met from the record.

tests.name: Engineering capacity, rule 6 and the engineering ring-fence, plan B. A failure would be a red line.
tests.threshold: One new launch per round. A development overlap between NGSA and an A350 Re-engine of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more. A named widebody team that draws nothing from NGSA in-service support, the A320neo transition or the engine durability work.

tests.name: Production readiness: a widebody engine ready by the A350 Re-engine's entry into service, plan B. This is a soft-veto ground; the board does not price it.
tests.threshold: Launch an A350 Re-engine only with a named engine on the record that is ready at or before the airframe's entry into service. This is rule 1's discipline for NGSA (no entry into service before the technology is ready) applied to the widebody.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time so that entry into service stays at or after the new technology-ready year. Never cancel.
tests.numbers: No slip is reported, and every NGSA engine is in service. The A350 Re-engine's problem is not a slip: no widebody engine has been committed in time (see the readiness test).

tests.name: Rule 1 and NGSA readiness. This is a red line.
tests.threshold: No NGSA entry into service before the 2035 technology-ready year. Any durability flag is answered through supply and fleet action, not by re-timing NGSA.
tests.numbers: NGSA entered service in 2037, two years after 2035. ngsa is hold only, and no cancel is on the menu, so nothing in 2050 re-times it.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No programme reaction to Boeing's rate. We keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on the record, and the order existed only in 2030. Boeing's fps ramp (860 deliveries in 2045, 940 in 2049) changes none of our orders.

vetoes.plan: B. Plan A plus an A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 (entry into service 2055).
vetoes.ground:
Production readiness, a soft veto. No widebody engine on the record is ready by a 2055 entry into service.
- Rolls-Royce, the A350 incumbent, spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine.
- An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, one year late.
- No fallback engine is on the record.

Grid margin against the best option that passes my tests (A, hold): +0.57 in S1 and -0.41 in S2. That is under $1B in both columns, so the team's override rule cannot carry B. The override budget is intact, unused in rounds 1 to 3, but it cannot be used here.

This is not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result.

In 2045 this veto moved the window. In the last decision year there is no later round in which to re-test, so it closes the board's widebody case. The gate failed in both 2045 and 2050 on the same one-year gap between engine and airframe. A350 family studies continue as staged studies.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. A widebody engine on the record that is ready by 2055. That could be Rolls-Royce committing UltraFan WB, or a Trent XWB derivative, with a ready date of 2055 or earlier, or a second maker offering an engine. Readiness would then pass, and the launch would turn on the grid tests (the $1B launch test and Toepfer's gate), which are not mine. On this grid, where +0.57 is the ceiling, it would still fail those.

2. Line data confirming that the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate. That would strengthen a future case beyond the game, but it does not change 2050.

3. A durability flag from any maker on the NGSA fleet, a supply crunch, a quality escape, or a problem on the NGSA line or the A320neo transition. Each of these only strengthens hold: B would fail outright as a safety, ramp or supply result, which no one overrides. The response would be supply and fleet action, never an NGSA re-timing or cancel.

4. My read of Boeing does not change my result. It rests on the engine, not on S2.
ops.memo:
My tests come from my role, not from anything I have said on record. Confidence: Very low.

I recommend plan A: NGSA hold, engine code None, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none.

Safety and quality: pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality, durability or supply problem. No engine maker has raised a flag. CFM's hot-and-harsh remark is labelled "not a flag", and I do not read it as one. The brief gives no time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit figures for either NGSA engine family, so I cannot report them. The fleet record goes to the safety review with my NGSA line and A320neo transition reports.

Ramp: pass. 1,060 deliveries a year from 2049 reflects share, not a line problem. Supply crunch: not applicable. Joint Venture: unchanged, with CFM as backstop within resized needs.

A350 Re-engine: capacity passes, with no overlap, $0 strain and one launch. The A350F and Spirit pass on the game proxy only; the record is silent after 2025. Readiness fails again. Rolls-Royce spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched with us is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. No fallback is on the record.

That is a soft veto, binding: +0.57 / -0.41 against hold, under $1B in both columns, so no override carries it. It is not a safety or ramp result. In the last decision year it closes the board's widebody case on the same one-year gap as 2045.

other_moves.move: Twice-yearly safety review: the NGSA line, the A320neo transition and the in-service durability record of both NGSA engine families, taken as one package
other_moves.detail:
This is the Board's priority 1 and recommendation 4, adopted as written. Wagner brings three reports to every review:
- his NGSA line report;
- the A320neo transition report;
- the in-service durability record of the CFM ducted and the P&W-RR Joint Venture engines on NGSA: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits.

The brief gives no figures for any of these, so the record is silent. Each maker reports on field data, and each report enters the review as soon as it is published.

No flag is on the record. CFM's hot-and-harsh remark is labelled "not a flag", and neither Wagner nor I read it as one. P&W's Hot Section kit and its undated GTF recovery stay a watch item on the A320neo fleet, not a flag.

Any flag from any maker comes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. It is answered through supply and fleet action: root cause, inspection, a parts fix, then shop visits and spares. It is never answered by re-timing NGSA.

The Joint Venture watch item stays on the agenda: two of our three makers ride on one engine, and CFM is the backstop within our resized needs, never as extra slots [AX-0015, AX-0056, AX-0081, A-0303, A-0331, AG-0038, AG-0067, AG-0068].

other_moves.move: Supply agreements sized to our own needs: the ECSC reports the outcome of the 2045 resizing
Closing record of the staged A350 Re-engine case
other_moves.detail:
This is the Board's item (7). The case closes on the board at hold, gate by gate:
- **Rule 3:** met throughout the game; no 787 Re-engine is on the record. A Boeing launch in the same year would have been the S2 column, not a launch after Boeing.
- **A350F and Spirit A350 packages:** pass on the game proxy only (2050 is well past the 2033-35 window). The line record is silent after 2025.
- **Widebody engine ready by entry into service:** failed in 2045 and again in 2050. The gap is the same one year each time (UltraFan WB at launch + 6, the airframe at launch + 5), and no fallback engine is on the record.
- **Grid gate (at least $1B in the expected column, not negative in the 787 Re-engine column):** failed at +0.89 / -0.50 in 2045 and at +0.57 / -0.41 in 2050.
- **Peak cash:** passed both times ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom).
- **Qualified Majority:** not sought.

Lesson for the portfolio, as Wagner states it: an engine gap built into the clocks closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe. Off the board, the A350 family's future continues as staged studies [A-0302, AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0364].

ECSC integrity review: supply sizing, hiring and pricing
Capital allocation inside the policy

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Our first task now is the fleet in service. We put fleet safety and operational integrity above all, and with our engine partners we follow how these engines perform in service, on field data. We continue production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We continue to study the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock, and we will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before. We also continue to prepare the technologies for the generations of aircraft that will follow.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes, and we keep recruiting the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
**Decision: plan A, the company default.** NGSA hold, engine code None, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. Grid +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2; expected PV about $23.36B at my 30% for S2. There is no Board item.

**Team rule, step by step**
1. **Delete red-line and pillars breaches.** Neither plan breaks a company red line:
   - Rule 1 is met: NGSA entered service in 2037.
   - Rules 2 and 7: no cancel is on the menu.
   - Rule 3 is not binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
   - Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are none, the only value.
   - Rule 6 is met: plan B would be one launch with 0 years of overlap.
   - Both plans stand on the five pillars on the record. Wagner adds that plan B could do so only with a public window the engine can meet; 2055 would overstate a 2056 engine.
2. **Survivors.**
   - Plan A passes both colleagues' tests.
   - Plan B fails Toepfer's added-move gate, which is also the company's $1B A350 Re-engine launch test (profile section 6): +0.57 in S1, $0.43B short, and -0.41 in S2.
   - Plan B also fails Wagner's production-readiness test. No widebody engine is on the record for a 2055 entry into service: an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, and no fallback exists.
   - Both are soft vetoes, and both colleagues mark them binding. Plan A is the only survivor.
3. **Highest survivor, and the doctrine default.** In my expected column (S1) the best grid row is plan B at +23.94. Hold is $0.57B below it, inside the $1B doctrine default, so I take the default even before the vetoes. The tie-breaks all point the same way: no added entry into service, no strain, no capex start, and fewer Board items.
4. **Override.** None is available, and none is used. Plan B is not $1B better than the best passing option: it leads by +0.57 in S1 and trails by -0.41 in S2. The Board's override review would also fail it. The game's one override closes unused.

**Read of Boeing (the Board's recommendation 1).** I put S2 at about 30%, within a range of 20-40%, down from 40% in 2045.
- Against S2, Boeing said "We're not launching a new program today" and "Today all three aren't there", gave no date, and put debt reduction "far and away" first. Its fps ramp is still KPI-gated, and Rolls-Royce spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine.
- For S2: Charleston has headroom, readiness work on the 787's next step continues, and this is the last decision year.
- S2 therefore stays the worst plausible column.
- At 30% the item is worth about +0.28. It is +0.33 at 25%, +0.18 at 40% and +0.08 at 50%, and it breaks even at 58%.
- My answer does not rest on this read: the item's ceiling is +0.57 at 0% for S2, which is below $1B. We decide on our own clock and our own tests.

**Last decision year.** No later round exists. A launch could not be gated, re-tested or cancelled on the board. The cancel condition cannot be reached either, because a 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 cannot enter service before 2055. Proof comes before commitment [AX-0007, AX-0008, A-0364], and the proof is missing on engine, value and line data. Toepfer's check of the option to wait shows that waiting bought the same case, smaller (+0.61 estimated against +0.57 on the grid) and with a heavier relative downside: break-even fell from 64% to 58%.

**In the order I am paid to protect**
- **Pillars.** The task is a fleet in service, with two new engine families in hot and harsh service and no durability claim yet from any maker. Hold adds nothing that could draw on the people, shops or supplier slots behind that work [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0015].
- **Ramp.** The NGSA line runs at 1,060 a year with the A320neo transition, under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010].
- **The Airbus of the 2030s.** That aircraft was delivered, NGSA on its clock in 2037. My instinct favours the widebody derivative, but this case clears neither our engine test nor our value test. The long view continues as staged studies.
- **The Board.** It approves hold as readily as a launch.

**Board-gate lines.** No order differs from the default, so no Board item is submitted. For the record, plan B would have read:
- five pillars: pass, conditional on its window;
- Toepfer: fail (soft veto, binding);
- Wagner: fail on production readiness (soft veto, binding);
- grid ΔPV: +0.57 / -0.41 against hold.
It would also have met the Board's would-veto ground on an unresolved binding ExCo veto. The Board would have nothing to vote, so plan B is not submitted.

**Cost of the decision.** Holding gives up $0.57B in S1, about $0.28B in expectation, and gains $0.41B in S2. Its worst column (+23.33) beats plan B's (+22.92). No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Our first task now is the fleet in service. We put fleet safety and operational integrity above all, and with our engine partners we follow how these engines perform in service, on field data. We continue production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We continue to study the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock, and we will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before. We also continue to prepare the technologies for the generations of aircraft that will follow.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes, and we keep recruiting the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
final.rationale:
**Decision: plan A, the company default.** NGSA hold, engine code None, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. Grid +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2; expected PV about $23.36B at my 30% for S2. There is no Board item.

**Team rule, step by step**
1. **Delete red-line and pillars breaches.** Neither plan breaks a company red line:
   - Rule 1 is met: NGSA entered service in 2037.
   - Rules 2 and 7: no cancel is on the menu.
   - Rule 3 is not binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
   - Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are none, the only value.
   - Rule 6 is met: plan B would be one launch with 0 years of overlap.
   - Both plans stand on the five pillars on the record. Wagner adds that plan B could do so only with a public window the engine can meet; 2055 would overstate a 2056 engine.
2. **Survivors.**
   - Plan A passes both colleagues' tests.
   - Plan B fails Toepfer's added-move gate, which is also the company's $1B A350 Re-engine launch test (profile section 6): +0.57 in S1, $0.43B short, and -0.41 in S2.
   - Plan B also fails Wagner's production-readiness test. No widebody engine is on the record for a 2055 entry into service: an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, and no fallback exists.
   - Both are soft vetoes, and both colleagues mark them binding. Plan A is the only survivor.
3. **Highest survivor, and the doctrine default.** In my expected column (S1) the best grid row is plan B at +23.94. Hold is $0.57B below it, inside the $1B doctrine default, so I take the default even before the vetoes. The tie-breaks all point the same way: no added entry into service, no strain, no capex start, and fewer Board items.
4. **Override.** None is available, and none is used. Plan B is not $1B better than the best passing option: it leads by +0.57 in S1 and trails by -0.41 in S2. The Board's override review would also fail it. The game's one override closes unused.

**Read of Boeing (the Board's recommendation 1).** I put S2 at about 30%, within a range of 20-40%, down from 40% in 2045.
- Against S2, Boeing said "We're not launching a new program today" and "Today all three aren't there", gave no date, and put debt reduction "far and away" first. Its fps ramp is still KPI-gated, and Rolls-Royce spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine.
- For S2: Charleston has headroom, readiness work on the 787's next step continues, and this is the last decision year.
- S2 therefore stays the worst plausible column.
- At 30% the item is worth about +0.28. It is +0.33 at 25%, +0.18 at 40% and +0.08 at 50%, and it breaks even at 58%.
- My answer does not rest on this read: the item's ceiling is +0.57 at 0% for S2, which is below $1B. We decide on our own clock and our own tests.

**Last decision year.** No later round exists. A launch could not be gated, re-tested or cancelled on the board. The cancel condition cannot be reached either, because a 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 cannot enter service before 2055. Proof comes before commitment [AX-0007, AX-0008, A-0364], and the proof is missing on engine, value and line data. Toepfer's check of the option to wait shows that waiting bought the same case, smaller (+0.61 estimated against +0.57 on the grid) and with a heavier relative downside: break-even fell from 64% to 58%.

**In the order I am paid to protect**
- **Pillars.** The task is a fleet in service, with two new engine families in hot and harsh service and no durability claim yet from any maker. Hold adds nothing that could draw on the people, shops or supplier slots behind that work [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0015].
- **Ramp.** The NGSA line runs at 1,060 a year with the A320neo transition, under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010].
- **The Airbus of the 2030s.** That aircraft was delivered, NGSA on its clock in 2037. My instinct favours the widebody derivative, but this case clears neither our engine test nor our value test. The long view continues as staged studies.
- **The Board.** It approves hold as readily as a launch.

**Board-gate lines.** No order differs from the default, so no Board item is submitted. For the record, plan B would have read:
- five pillars: pass, conditional on its window;
- Toepfer: fail (soft veto, binding);
- Wagner: fail on production readiness (soft veto, binding);
- grid ΔPV: +0.57 / -0.41 against hold.
It would also have met the Board's would-veto ground on an unresolved binding ExCo veto. The Board would have nothing to vote, so plan B is not submitted.

**Cost of the decision.** Holding gives up $0.57B in S1, about $0.28B in expectation, and gains $0.41B in S2. Its worst column (+23.33) beats plan B's (+22.92). No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective.

final.objective_note:
The briefing goal is "Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family". It is scored by the GM and never part of the payoff.
- **Protect the A320 family: met.** Share was 60% in every year before NGSA entered service in 2037.
- **Defend the 60/40 edge: not met.** Share was 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050, on the long-run 47/53 split after fps entered service.
- No order on this round's menu moves narrowbody share. Delay Tactics are closed, and the A350 Re-engine is a widebody item.

final.predictions:
**Boeing**
- About 70%: it holds the 787 in 2050 with no Re-engine launch, keeps the fps ramp KPI-gated toward the long-run 47% narrowbody share, and keeps debt reduction first.
- About 30% (S2): it launches a 787 Re-engine. That could enter service no earlier than 2055, and it costs us only about $0.04B on the grid under hold.

**Our position**

board_response.recommendation: 1. Decide the A350 Re-engine on the ExCo's own tests and an explicit read of Boeing, with a probability on S2.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- My S2 probability is about 30%, within a range of 20-40%, reasoned from the bulletin: Boeing gave no date, said it is "not launching a new program today" and that "all three aren't there", and put debt first. Charleston's headroom and the continuing readiness work keep S2 plausible.
- At 30% the item is worth about +0.28, against a break-even of 58%.
- Both of my colleagues' tests fail the launch: Toepfer's added-move gate and Wagner's production readiness. Both are binding soft vetoes, and no override is available.
- The answer is hold. It does not rest on the read of Boeing, because +0.57 at 0% for S2 is still below $1B.

board_response.recommendation: 2. Treat 2050 as the last decision year; proof first. If launched: an annual Audit Committee cash gate, the write-off schedule, and a cancel condition that cannot be reached.
board_response.response:
Taken up. This is decisive in my rationale: a launch now would be an unconditional commitment through 2055 with no gate on the board, and the proof is missing on engine, value and line data.

Toepfer confirms the cancel condition cannot be reached: a 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 enters service in 2055 at the earliest, so never first.

The governance is recorded but not triggered, because we hold:
- an annual Audit Committee cash gate at $1.0B a year;
- write-off of $5B x years elapsed / 5, shown in reported EBIT and never adjusted away.

board_response.recommendation: 3. Engine path: Wagner names the engine, its readiness and the fallback; not a veto ground on its own unless a readiness failure is overridden.
board_response.response:
Taken up. Wagner names Rolls-Royce, the A350 incumbent, as the only path.
- An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service.
- No Trent XWB derivative with a ready date and no second maker is on the record.
- He fails the launch on production readiness: a soft veto, binding, on the same one-year gap as in 2045.

I did not override it, so no overridden readiness failure comes to the Board. His lesson goes into the closing record and the A350 studies: the gap closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe.

board_response.recommendation: 4. Safety, durability and the NGSA line: three reports as one package at the twice-yearly safety review; the Joint Venture watch item; any flag to the Board first, answered through supply and fleet action; the ring-fence.
board_response.response:
Adopted as written.

Wagner brings three reports to every review as one package: the NGSA line report, the A320neo transition report, and the durability record of both NGSA engine families.
- No flag is on the record, and he does not read CFM's hot-and-harsh remark as one.
- The brief gives no time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit figures, so the record is silent. Each maker's field-data report enters the review when published.
- The Joint Venture watch item stays on the agenda, with CFM as the backstop within our resized needs.

Any flag reaches the Board before the cash line and is answered through supply and fleet action, never by re-timing NGSA. Hold adds nothing that draws on those people, shops or slots.

board_response.recommendation: 5. Returns and rating: payout 30-50%, buyback room under the AGM authority after programme cash, base case beside stress case, A+/A1 headroom proxy; no equity raise; state support upside only.
board_response.response:
Taken up on Toepfer's schedule.
- Under hold, programme cash is nil.
- At a 50% payout, buyback room is about $4.78B a year in the base case and $2.36B in the stress case.
- The net-cash proxy stays positive every year in both cases.
- The 18-month AGM authority caps holdings at 10% of issued capital. Its dollar size is not in our record, because the share price is not.
- The agencies' thresholds are still not in our record, so A+/A1 headroom is shown as a proxy: net cash at or above zero, and programme spend at 0% of the line.
- There is no equity raise and no dividend cut, and state money is upside only, never assumed in the case.

board_response.recommendation: 6. Integrity and the briefing objective: 60/40 not met, no value or integrity traded for it; the ECSC reports the supply resizing, hiring and pricing; Delay Tactics stay none.
board_response.response:
Agreed and taken up.
- The 60/40 edge is not met (53% in 2050); A320 family protection is met. No order moves share, and no PV or integrity is traded for the objective.
- The ECSC reports each resized agreement (engines from all three makers, wing packages, titanium, rare earths), sized to 1,060 a year and never held at the 2039 peak. Any agreement above EUR 300m comes to the Board. The brief gives no values, so none is named yet.
- Hiring is open and never targets rival teams, and pricing stays within ordinary competition.
- Delay Tactics are none, and no unpriced move recreates them.

board_response.recommendation: 7. The long view: research and technology for the generation after NGSA and A350 family studies stay funded as staged studies below EUR 300m until a Board gate; reviewed at the annual off-site.
board_response.response:
Adopted. Research and technology for the generation after NGSA, A350 family studies, an NGSA derivative study and an A220 variant study continue as staged studies inside the Board-approved R&D budget.
- Each stays below EUR 300m of committed spend until a Board gate.
- Toepfer proposes an aggregate cap of about EUR 1.2bn over the study phase, roughly $0.35B a year. That is his inference, since the record gives no study sizes.
- Any item crossing EUR 300m comes to the Board, and any launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority.
- The annual off-site reviews the portfolio. None is presented as a launch.

board_response.recommendation: 8. Public statement: lead with the five pillars and NGSA fleet safety and durability; windows, not dates; if held, the A350 family including the A350F remains the focus on Airbus's own clock, committing to nothing either way; no Boeing reference; never Delay Tactics.
board_response.response:
Complied.
- The statement opens with the five pillars, then fleet safety and in-service performance on field data. It makes no durability claim.
- It gives windows only ("since the second half of the 2030s").
- It keeps the A350 family, including the A350F, as our focus on our own technology and industrial clock, committing to nothing either way.
- It makes no reference to Boeing and never mentions Delay Tactics.
- Toepfer's finance line is used as written.
The Board vets the final text [AX-0004].

recommendations.text:
Hold the 787 Re-engine.

Its item value is +0.05 / -1.00. It clears $1B in neither column, and in S2 it sits at our -$1B limit. Launched in the last decision year, H5 would lock that in with no exit. In S1, +0.05 is inside ε, and the tie goes to doing less, better and to the plan whose worst column is higher, by 1.00. Holding is the better call whenever the chance of S2 is above 4.8%.

Malave's round-3 estimate of about +0.04 tied out to the grid's +0.05. Record the forgone Re-engine as a loss accepted, not a wait.

On the 787's future:
- Grow it from Charleston.
- Keep the readiness work going without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements.
- Publish no Re-engine date.
- If Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine, H3's second half bars a 787 Re-engine from then on.

The Aerospace Safety Committee asks to hear directly, each year, from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. Their report should cover:
- fps in-service safety and reliability at 940 a year;
- the CFM ducted engine's durability on field data, with hot and harsh service first, as CFM has committed in public;
- supplier and quality KPIs;
- the 737 and 787 results.

On the line and the supply base:
- A CFM durability or allocation flag holds the next fps step until the fleet action is in place.
- Any step above 940 stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next.
- Certify before building at rate on any derivative, with no production-certification concurrency.
- Keep the CFM line, long-lead structures, titanium forgings and rare-earth parts contracted and funded for the rate in front of us, and track CFM allocation by airframer.
- Attribute nothing to anyone.

Disclosure and the long cycle, at the close.

Report the narrowbody path honestly: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045, and 47% from 2049 through 2060, the 47/53 long-run split. Both objectives stay recorded as not met. No order on offer can change that, so no objective premium applies.

Tie no order to Airbus in either direction: do not launch to pre-empt an A350 Re-engine, and do not hold because of one. The hold rests on ε and on debt first. We judge this plan on the long cycle, and we will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions.

Premium log and board_response.

The premium:
- If S1 is expected and the Re-engine is held, log 0.05 as a doctrine premium within ε. The cumulative total becomes 0.46 + 0 + 0.30 + 0.05 = 0.81 against the $2B cap.
- If S2 is expected, log 0, and the cumulative total stays at 0.76.

Keep hard-rule costs in their own log: H3 2.20 (round 1), H4 0.65 (round 2), none in rounds 3 and 4.

This is the last decision year, so answer every recommendation here in board_response, including those carried from rounds 2 and 3. Nothing can be raised again later.

frame.question:
2050 is the last decision year on this board. The fps has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave, and it holds 940 deliveries a year from 2049. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem.

Only one order is live: re787. A 787 Re-engine launched now would enter service in 2055. Does it earn a place? Or do we hold, keep doing less and doing it better, and accept that the Re-engine is forgone on this board?

Two things sit under that question, and I owe the Board both at the close: the KPI record on the fps at 940, and a straight funding report on debt and the rating.

My four questions to this ExCo:

It keeps the investment-grade year at 2053, but it cuts the room from $4.5B to $0.5B and gives up the 2052 upside. One year of certification slip costs about 0.09 before concessions and rework, which takes the item below zero. We can't meet and beat a baseline with no room for one year.

Operating profit came in on the path: 81.5 over 2045-49. On the conservative case debt was $60.9B at end-2049. The brief doesn't show the 2047 upside, so I don't claim it. Debt stays first, with no dividend or buyback proposal before the rating is solid.

I recommend Do Nothing. The premium is 0.05, cumulative 0.81 of $2B, barring a live problem or a profit shortfall.

tests.name: KPI gate for the 737 Rate Increase: my veto (doctrine; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, with 2-3 months of stability before the next. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: The 2050 brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and the bulletin carries no CFM durability or allocation flag. rate_737 is offered only at hold, so the veto has nothing to bind: I checked it and do not invoke it. For the record, on all three lines: the fps delivered 860 in 2045, then 880, 900, 920 and 940 in 2049, exactly the briefed path. It holds at 940 through 2060. The 787 is flat at 100 a year (58.8%). Operating profit came in at 15.7-16.9 over 2045-49, 81.5 in total, on the path. The board carries deliveries, not KPIs. The KPI record (stable months at rate, quality escapes, FAA findings) comes directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to Aerospace Safety, and I do not substitute delivery counts for it. Nothing in the board's numbers contradicts stability: no dip, no slip, no flag.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: Do Nothing, fps in service (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? No column is labelled 'Risk case' this year, because the fps is in service and has no slip leg. So I read each plan's worst column and say how much of its value rests on a nominal date.
tests.numbers: The fps entered service in 2040, on its date. Share ran the plan path at 1 pp a year: 38% in 2040, 43% in 2045, 47% from 2049, the 47/53 long-run split for 3 years of lead. Do Nothing's worst column is S2 at +0.57, against B's -0.43. None of A's value rests on a future EIS; it rests on the line holding 940. Sensitivity: each point of narrowbody share is 20 fps a year x $55M x 25.64% = $0.28B a year of operating profit, nominal.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: 787 Re-engine with EIS 2055, row B (record [BX-1331] by inference; doctrine slip prior)
tests.threshold: Same test. I add doctrine's slip prior for a major derivative: central +2 years, range +1 to +4 (profile.md, inference). Certifying before building at rate moves the date. It does not let the line build ahead.
tests.numbers: B's worst column is -0.43 in S2, 1.00 below A's +0.57. The board fixes EIS at launch + 5 = 2055, with no headroom. The record runs both ways: the MAX 8 came early on a conservative date [B-0535], while the 777X and MAX 10 ran 6-7 years late [B-1498, B-2243]. My reconstruction of the S1 operating gain ties to Malave's round-3 build of about +0.76 PV. Margin uplift is 100 x $180M x 5.21 pp = $0.94B a year nominal. Share adds 1 pp a year of widebody (1.7 airplanes x $180M x 25.21% = $0.077B a year per point). Both run over 20 years from 2055, and the $180M is the brief's 2026 revenue less 800 x $48M, over 100. One year of slip defers about 0.07 of that gain (0.76 x 0.095), which is more than the item's whole +0.05. On the board the bill (0.28 PV) and penalty (0.44) move with EIS, so the mechanical net is near zero. Any real cost of slip (concessions, rework, carrying cost) turns the S1 item negative. So all of B's S1 value rests on the nominal 2055 date. In S2 the 787 margin falls from 20% to 15.77%, $0.76B a year nominal, and a slip of ours would leave an A350 Re-engine alone from 2055, gaining 1.5 pp a year until we enter service. Malave costs the slip all-in.

tests.name: fps line at 940: stability, steps and supplier readiness (doctrine; CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: Every step KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA: steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, with 2-3 months of stability before the next. Supplier readiness is a hard gate. Fragile suppliers stay funded and hot for the rate in front of us. Name categories, not companies, and attribute nothing.
tests.numbers: The ramp ran 860 to 940 over 2045-49. That is +20 a year, or +1.67 a month each year: about one step of 5 every three years, 17% of doctrine's maximum tempo of two steps a year. 940 a year is about 78 a month on the board's stylised volumes, so I read it in relative terms. The board holds us flat at 940 (47% of 2,000) through 2060. So on the board, demand calls for no step above 940 (capacity follows visible demand [BX-1329], inference). Any step above it is unpriced and stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. Stable months, quality escapes and FAA findings are the Chief Engineer's to report. At a flat rate the in-service tail binds, not a step. About 8,500 fps were delivered in 2040-49 (17,000 engines), rising to about 14,100 by 2055 as shop visits come due. Binding order (inference from doctrine): (1) the CFM engine line, sole source, carrying OE engines and Ducted spares; (2) long-lead airframe structures [B-1449, B-2097]; (3) titanium forgings and (4) rare-earth parts, which are shared and finite. The bulletin shows another airframer resizing its agreements in these categories to its own needs (1,060 narrowbodies from 2049). That is an ordinary market move, which if anything eases shared capacity; no attribution. Keep all four funded and hot for 940 plus spares, not contracted above it (working capital, my record [BX-1327]). Embed staff at any supplier that falls behind.

tests.name: Engines: CFM allocation and CFM ducted durability in service (doctrine; CEO ask 3; not priced on the board)
tests.threshold: No durability or safety flag in service. Boeing's engine need is tracked against the maker's output across both airframers and the aftermarket. Durability is shown only on field data.
tests.numbers: Allocation (bulletin arithmetic): CFM had 56.8% of 4,000 narrowbody engines in 2049, or 2,272. We took 940 x 2 = 1,880 of them, 82.7%, up from 1,680 of 2,148 (78.2%) in 2044. That leaves 392 OE engines for NGSA and the A320neo. The CEO's 83% is right. On 'contracted': our round-3 move contracts delivery commitments for each step. The board carries no contract data, so I confirm the process, not the paper. On 'safe': there is no allocation flag. CFM says publicly that spares never crowd out OE engines, and the other airframer's resized engine agreements lower competing calls on the line. The exposure is concentration: one sole-source line carries 100% of our narrowbody deliveries, and we take 83% of its output. Track it by airframer [B-1923]. LEAP-1B spares for the 737 fleet are off the board. Durability: CFM ducted has been in service since 2036 (14 years), and on the fps since 2040 (10 years), with no flag on the record. But in CFM's own public words, 'what we don't know yet is how these new engines hold up over years of service', and it makes no durability claim before field data. So it is not flagged, and not yet shown. Time on wing on field data, hot and harsh service first, is the Chief Engineer's to report to Aerospace Safety. A flag holds any step above 940.

tests.name: 737 and 787 results, and customer trust at 940 (doctrine; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: KPI and safety results come directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. Deliver on the dates promised, and make every transaction build trust.
tests.numbers: 787: 100 a year at a 20% margin is $3.6B a year of operating profit (100 x $180M x 20%), flat through 2060, with no live problem in the brief. 737: the brief's revenue reconciles to every Boeing narrowbody at the fps price (2049: 940 x $55M + $18.0B = $69.7B). So on the board the 737 MAX has no new-build deliveries, and its results are fleet and LEAP-1B spares, which are off the board. The quality, FAA and safety results belong to the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. I give the board's delivery record, not a substitute for theirs. Customer trust at 940: quote slots only against the KPI-gated line, never an earlier internal number [BX-1273, B-2315]. Deliver spares and support on time to the in-service fleet of about 8,500 fps, because on-time, predictable delivery covers services too (my record [BX-1331], applied by inference).

tests.name: Two-front strain (engineering capacity), row B (doctrine; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS. Any derivative certifies before it builds at rate.
tests.numbers: The fps counted 2033-40, and a Re-engine launched in 2050 counts 2050-55. Overlap is 0 years and strain $0, 2 years inside H4. The fps development engineers were released at EIS 2040, and doctrine's 2.5 years to design rate puts the handover around 2042-43 (inference). A Re-engine would feather in on the back side [B-1393, B-0341] without pulling people off the line, because the line at 940 is production, supplier and FAA work. The board does not price two loads: FAA certification bandwidth, the pacing item since 2019 [B-2343], and in-service engineering support for about 8,500 fps on a 10-year-old engine. I confirm certify-before-rate as a condition, with no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]. It moves the date, not the line.

tests.name: Technology readiness for a 2055 EIS (doctrine; CEO ask 6; advice, not a veto ground, not priced on the board)
tests.threshold: A new widebody engine, matured, with durability shown, ready by the Re-engine's EIS of 2055.
tests.numbers: On the public record, the upgraded GEnx has flown on the 787 since 2033. It is the airplane's current engine, so a Re-engine on it adds no new engine. Doctrine's choice, a GEnx derivative (profile.md), has no durability record until it is built and tested. UltraFan WB is ready 6 years after launch, so if launched now it is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 EIS. Rolls-Royce also says it spends nothing new on a widebody engine without a Re-engine, and this is the last sealed round, so no later launch exists. CFM calls RISE technology, with no product date. No engine on the record meets the threshold, and the technology work stream has not converged [BX-1296].

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the IP. Partner only where the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: A Re-engine would be a Solo airframe derivative with an engine partner, and that is the right split. The 787 airframe IP is Boeing's. Boeing owns no engine IP, so the engine is a partner's in every case. I see no reason to do it otherwise. The board offers no Re-engine Joint Venture, and the 787's risk-sharing lesson is to wall off critical technology [B-0361, B-0386]. The fps stays Solo, in service on CFM.

tests.name: Widebody capacity at Charleston (inference [BX-1329]; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Add capacity where demand on the grid is visible. Charleston must carry the 787 with or without a Re-engine.
tests.numbers: Without a Re-engine, the board holds the 787 at 100 a year (58.8% of 170), or 8.3 a month, through 2060. The Charleston expansion is built for rates above 10 a month and into the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. With a Re-engine alone (S1), +1 pp a year from 2055 gives about 110 a year by 2060, or 9.2 a month, still under 10. In S2 nothing moves. So Charleston can grow the 787 with or without a Re-engine. The board shows no demand above 100 a year; any growth beyond it is commercial and unpriced.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number with a sensitivity per unit.
tests.numbers: A has no new bill. It runs 16.9 a year of operating profit, 10.2 above the status quo, all available to debt. B books $5B at EIS 2055, about 0.28 PV. Real spend is about $1.0B a year over 2050-54 (inference): 5.9% of operating profit and 9.8% of the uplift. Its debt penalty is +$3.10B undiscounted on top of the fps's $105.32B. That is $0.62B of penalty per $1B spent beside the fps debt, against $0.12B per $1B ($0.6B in all) for a Re-engine alone. In PV it is about 0.44 on Malave's build, already inside the grid and never subtracted again. B is fundable from operations with no new equity. On the CEO's arithmetic, debt runs down 4.1 a year with B instead of 5.1, reaching about $44.5B at end-2053, with $0.5B of room. Whether that moves the investment-grade year is Malave's call. A converts cash best.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers: No ramp order is offered. The fps has been in service since 2040 on the 10-year ramp, with $60.32B booked at EIS. The board offers fps: hold only.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase (inference [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it, in the expected column.
tests.numbers: rate_737 is offered only at hold, and the grid has no Rate Increase row. The 2030 round was the only one that offered it.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (any combination)
vetoes.ground: KPI veto checked and NOT invoked. The order is not offered this round (hold only), and the 2050 brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. Neither condition of the team rule's veto holds, so nothing binds. If a live problem appears, the veto binds against any Rate Increase. I would also ask that the fps line hold at its current rate until the KPIs show 2-3 months of stability.

vetoes.plan: fps: hold + re787: launch (row B)
vetoes.ground: Not my veto, and no hard-rule breach. H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. H4: 0 years of overlap (fps 2033-40, Re-engine 2050-55), so $0 of strain. H5: once launched, a Re-engine is never cancelled. In this last round, an A350 Re-engine launched in the same sealed round would lock in S2's -1.00 with no exit. H6: not in play. Advice only, not binding: (1) technology readiness fails, because no widebody engine with durability shown can be ready by 2055 and UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2056; (2) all of the S1 item's +0.05 rests on the nominal date, since one year of slip defers about 0.07 of operating gain; (3) its worst column is -0.43, against Do Nothing's +0.57. I recommend hold.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Three things would change my view. (1) A live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, reported in the brief or by the Chief Engineer or the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. The KPI veto would bind against any Rate Increase (none is offered), and I would ask the fps line to hold at its current rate until the KPIs show 2-3 months of stability, with staff embedded at any supplier that falls behind. (2) A CFM ducted durability or allocation flag. I would hold any step above 940 and put the fleet action ahead of rate: root cause, inspection, parts fix, shop visits and spares. (3) For the 787 Re-engine, all four of these together: no A350 Re-engine on the record (H3); an item value above $1B in the expected column with no column below -$1B; a widebody engine with durability shown that can be ready by 2055 (a launched UltraFan WB ready by EIS, or a GEnx derivative with test results); and a planning date with headroom against doctrine's +2-year derivative prior, so that one year of slip (about 0.07 of operating gain) does not consume the item. My strain, capacity and IP tests already pass. None of these can arise on this board before the close, so I recommend all four holds.
ops.memo:
My record is thin: two Global Services events, nothing from BCA. Delivery, cash and IP are my record, applied by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time, predictable delivery. The fps came in on its date, and the line ran the plan path: 860 to 940 over 2045-49, 81.5 of operating profit, no dip, no flag. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The rate is hold only, so my KPI veto is checked and not invoked. The KPI record itself comes from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer, not delivery counts.

Second, the line at 940. The board holds us flat through 2060, so demand calls for no step above it. What binds now is the in-service tail: 8,500 fps, and 1,880 of CFM's 2,272 narrowbody engines, 83%. No durability flag, but by CFM's own word durability is not yet shown. Keep the CFM line, structures, titanium forgings and rare earths funded for 940 plus spares, not above it.

Third, the Re-engine. Strain is zero; capacity passes. Technology does not: no matured widebody engine for 2055. One year of slip defers about 0.07 of operating gain, more than the item's whole +0.05. In S2 it loses 1.00, locked in.

And finally, cash. $1.0B a year is 5.9% of operating profit, but each $1B beside the fps debt carries $0.62B of penalty, against $0.12B alone. Do Nothing converts best.

Orders: all four holds.

We track allocation across the fps, NGSA, the A320neo and 737 LEAP-1B spares, and keep delivery commitments contracted for the rate in front of us [BX-1264, BX-1325, B-1923].

decision.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It came in on the date we gave you. The line is at 940 airplanes a year, and we got there one step at a time: on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line had shown it was stable at the rate it was on. If we take another step, it works the same way.

We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 47%. That's up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and it's still short of half. I won't dress it up. We earn every point one delivery at a time, and that includes supporting the airplanes our customers already fly.

We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step again. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready, and today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched.

Paying down debt is still far and away our priority. We fund the business from our operations, with no new equity, and I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers.

Some things don't change. We certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us, and we keep working with CFM, our engine partner, on time on wing and support for the fleet.

A while back I said we were turning this big ship, but it hadn't turned yet. We've come a long way since then. There's still work to do, and we'll keep doing it the same way: do less, do it better, and let our own readiness set the pace. The financials will follow our production performance.
decision.rationale:
**Decision: Do Nothing.**
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- Row: +0.66 / +0.57 (S1 / S2).
- Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.

**1. The team rule, applied.**
- **Malave's buffer test: not applicable.** The brief labels no column 'Risk case', and the fps has been in service since 2040, so it has no slip leg. He confirms he holds no veto, and no plan is out on this ground.
- **The Board's S2 proxy** (floor 0.57 - 2.00 = -1.43): A passes by 2.00 and B by 1.00.
- **KPI doctrine (Pope's seat): not in play.** rate_737 is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. She checked her veto and did not invoke it.
- Neither colleague flagged a red line. I override nothing. The rest is my call.

**2. The grid** (round4.md §3):
- A, Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.57.
- B, fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.71 / -0.43.
- B's item is +0.05 / -1.00. Holding is the better call whenever the chance of S2 is above 4.8% (0.05 / 1.05).
- Malave's independent rebuild gives +0.042 / -1.001 (operating gain +0.758, bill -0.276, penalty -0.439). That ties to the grid and to his round-3 estimate of about +0.04. Pope's rebuild of the operating gain ties as well.

**3. My tests.**
- **KPI stability: pass.** No live problem in the brief, and no dip in the numbers: 860 to 940 over 2045-49, exactly on the path. Delivery counts are not KPIs, so the record comes from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- **Three work streams: not converged** [BX-1296].
  - *Market:* S2 is plausible. If both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2055, share doesn't move and our 787 margin falls from 20% to 15.77%, about $0.76B a year.
  - *Technology:* Pope fails it, as advice. The upgraded GEnx has been the 787's engine since 2033. A GEnx derivative has no durability record. UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2056, after a 2055 EIS. RISE has no product date. My technology risk appetite is Low [BX-1298]. This isn't priced on the board and it isn't why I hold, but it means that work stream isn't there.
  - *Boeing:* fundable. About $1.0B a year is 5.9% of operating profit, with no new equity. Funding isn't the issue; the return is.
- **Debt before the next airplane: B fails.** A second development has to beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and B does it in neither column [BX-1305, B-2326].
  - B adds +$3.10B of undiscounted penalty on top of $105.32B of debt (I accept Malave's wording fix). That's about 0.44 PV, already inside the grid and never subtracted again. For scale, the fps 10-year's own undiscounted penalty is $19.1B.
  - B would keep the conservative investment-grade year at 2053, but it cuts the room from $4.5B to $0.5B and gives up the 2052 upside.
- **FAA process: pass.** No certification trouble is reported [BX-1309].
- **Certification slip:** there's no risk-case column, so this is for scale only.
  - Malave: one year of slip costs about 0.09 priced, which takes B's S1 item to about -0.05 before concessions and rework.
  - Pope: one year defers about 0.07 of gain, more than the whole item.
  - So all of B's S1 value rests on a nominal 2055 date with no headroom. I don't plan that way [BX-1318, BX-1319, BX-1275].
- **Doing less, better:** +0.05 in S1 is inside ε, so the plan with less to execute wins [BX-1239]. A is also the higher-confidence plan: its worst column is higher by 1.00 [BX-0548]. In S2, A leads outright by 1.00.
- **Airbus doesn't set the date.** I'm not holding because of Airbus, and I wouldn't launch to pre-empt it either [B-2313]. On the grid, entering service in the same year costs us 1.00, so B is no hedge. The hold rests on ε, debt first and readiness.
- **Premium cap:** 0.05 this round, 0.81 cumulative, against $2B.

**4. Hard rules and red lines.**
- H1: does not apply. The fps is in service; I lifted H1 in Round 1, with evidence.
- H2: cannot bind.
- H3, first half: lapsed after Round 1.
- H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. If Airbus launches one this round, we stand aside (company doctrine [B-0917, B-0858], not my record).
- H4: 0 years of overlap (fps 2033-40, a Re-engine 2050-55). It would pass, so it isn't binding.
- H5: the fps can't be cancelled. A launched Re-engine is never cancelled, so in this last round S2's -1.00 would have been locked in.
- H6: not in play. H7: no trigger.
- H8: 0.81 of $2B, logged.
- My own lines: none is tested by a hold. Certify before rate, no fixed-price development, no blame on the FAA, and no attribution all stand.

final.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It came in on the date we gave you. The line is at 940 airplanes a year, and we got there one step at a time: on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line had shown it was stable at the rate it was on. If we take another step, it works the same way.

We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 47%. That's up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and it's still short of half. I won't dress it up. We earn every point one delivery at a time, and that includes supporting the airplanes our customers already fly.

We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step again. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready, and today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched.

Paying down debt is still far and away our priority. We fund the business from our operations, with no new equity, and I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers.

Some things don't change. We certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us, and we keep working with CFM, our engine partner, on time on wing and support for the fleet.

A while back I said we were turning this big ship, but it hadn't turned yet. We've come a long way since then. There's still work to do, and we'll keep doing it the same way: do less, do it better, and let our own readiness set the pace. The financials will follow our production performance.

- Open Fan: -19.17, which is the $8B bill plus $11.17B of 35 pp penalty.
