(2) Penalty start. BOARD GUIDANCE asks you to confirm it. My arithmetic (inference): about $0.32B per raw point from 2050 to 2056 gives $11.19B and $6.39B. A 2051 start gives $9.29B, which does not match. So it starts in 2050.
Then give the effect on 'Dominate' in 2050 on renormalised shares. My figures: 23.5% with the Open Fan alone and 37.8% with Lobby, against 56.8% on hold.

(3) Premium in dollars. I expect:
- $0 this round, $0 of $4.0B for the game;
- the RISE allowance at $0 of $15B, closing unused;
- the objective premium I decline: $15.38B for the cheapest route and $19.17B for the Open Fan alone.
Then the near miss. BOARD GUIDANCE wants it explained. $15.38B sits under the $15B allowance plus the $2.0B round cap. Tell me whether you agree it still fails:
- the allowance is declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, and $15.38B is over $15B;
- doctrine's gate G1 needs a committed airframer, and there is none;
- it buys nothing toward 'Introduce' (ready in 2060);
- it costs us 'Dominate' in 2050.

(4) Capex and payout. Confirm $0 new R&D and $0 new strain, and that the 2030 package ($4B Ducted R&D plus $2B strain) is complete and booked. The full ~$2.5B a year of room should stand after returning at least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow [CX-0645], with no rating effect unless you see one.

(5) Booking. I booked -39.60 last round and the record held at -38.29. No widebody move came in 2045, so I said I'd raise toward -38.29, and not past it. A 2050 move by someone else is still possible in this sealed round. Your round-3 figures for a 2050 launch were about -$0.41B (Trent 1000 upgrade) and -$0.50B (UltraFan WB with a re-engine). Mine are $0.43B and $0.53B. My lean is to book about -38.80: S1 less the larger of the two, per our round-3 lesson to book a named negative risk. Would you hold there, go lower, or go to -38.29?
Also check the public rules for anything that could still touch our NB share from 2050 to 2056, such as a relaunched solo engine. The brief's single column says no; I'd rather hear it from you. Ducted durability and raw materials stay named and unsized unless Ali raises a flag. A flag lowers the booking.

(6) Terms. There is no price lever. Airbus is resizing its engine long-term agreements down to its own needs, and Boeing says it will work with CFM to support its rates. Any CFM answer is joint with Safran, on standard terms, with no concession and no rate published [CX-0184, CX-0609]. Flag any wording in my statement plan that reads as price or capacity talk.

(7) BOARD GUIDANCE to test against. It would veto open_fan launch, Open Fan + Lobby, Lobby alone, any premium above $0, and any use of the allowance. Tell me if hold everything trips any of your tests. I don't believe it does.

Hold is the best row in the only column at -38.29. Nothing else is additive, so nothing else gets ordered [CX-0301]. That means no Board item, $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, premium $0 ($0 of $4.0B for the game), and the RISE allowance closing unused at $0 of $15B.

EXPECTED COLUMN: S1 at weight 1.0. It is the backlog on the record, not a hoped-for order [CX-0248].

BOOKING: about -38.80. That is S1 less about $0.5B for a same-round widebody move, the larger of the two exclusive cases. Ghai may move it.

OPEN FAN: hold. It is -19.17 alone and -15.38 with Lobby, all bill and penalty, and ready in 2060. The $15.38B route is a near miss on arithmetic only. The allowance needs an airframer who wants RISE, and there isn't one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. It would also cost 'Dominate' in the year it is scored.

I'll name my bias. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) and the last-round itch both pull toward a launch for the objective. But admission buys a seat, both airplanes have been flying for a decade, and the seat isn't for sale. RISE stays whole as technology, all in on the physics [CX-0214], 50-50 with Safran, with no date, feeding LEAP and the Ducted [CX-0162]. Holding is not a cancel (H5).

SAFRAN GATE:
- Hold orders nothing new on CFM, so there is nothing to gate.
- An Open Fan with no airframer path is outside joint practice. A 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base, so there is no reason Safran would agree.
- Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but the point is moot.
- Any price, terms or capacity answer to either airframer is joint [CX-0184].
- GEnx is GE alone.

OTHER MOVES (unpriced):
- Ali's in-service report on field data, with Safran's engineers. Any flag carries its fleet action.
- LEAP and Ducted OE and spares on time on the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer. Spares never crowd out OE, and no rate is published [CX-0529, CX-0542, CX-0552].
- RISE whole, 50-50, no date.
- Answers on Airbus's long-term-agreement resize and Boeing's rate support, joint with Safran on standard terms [CX-0200].
- Supplier and raw-materials contracts sized to our own needs.
- GEnx 787 support; we don't get ahead of Boeing on the 787 [CX-0307].
- No reaction to rival news [CX-0580, CX-0609].

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND:
- A safety or durability flag: fleet action first, and the booking comes down.
- Ghai finding an error in my grid reading.
- An airframer asking for RISE. None can, inside this game.
Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444].

CLOSING STATEMENT PLAN:
- Safety first, and what we know and what we don't.
- The fleet reported in cycles on field data, with no durable-fleet claim.
- Engines and spares on time.
- The Ducted is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us, not the next generation.
- RISE: all in with Safran. When it enters service is 'really not for us to say'.
- No rival, no blame, no price, no rate, no date.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.

terms. There is no launch-era pricing and no concession, and CFM narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran. Capacity also goes to the partner under hard rule 7. cfo.memo:
Larry, your arithmetic holds; nothing to hide. Hold is -38.29, the best row in our only column. The Open Fan is -19.17 against hold: an $8B bill plus $11.17B of 35-point penalty. With Lobby it's -15.38: $9B plus $6.38B. Lobby beside it is +3.79; alone, -1.00. I reproduce both penalties within $0.02B only from a 2050 start, at about $0.32B a raw point. A 2051 start leaves $1.9B and $1.1B unexplained. Neither row adds strain; the $2B is already in hold. Dominate in 2050 falls from 56.8% to 23.5%, or 37.8% with Lobby.

Premium: $0 this round, $0 of $4.0B for the game, RISE allowance $0 of $15B. The $15.38B route fails. It is $0.38B over the allowance, which is the exception to the cap, not a base to stack it on. It has no airframer, and buys a 2060 engine for a count ending in 2056.

Capex: $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, $2.55B a year of room, payout whole.

Volumes: the airframers' numbers are already in our grid; 1,060 and 940 are 53% and 47% of 2,000. Fewer Airbus engines, but the good news is more Boeing ones: we hold 2,273 a year. Size suppliers to that, not the peak; publish none of it.

Booking: -38.80. The narrowbody is locked. The one rules corner, a rival solo relaunched for 2056, is about $0.19B, inside the $0.51B widebody cushion. A durability flag from Mohamed comes off in the round we find it.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (date veto ground 1): the ready year of every order and every grid row

tests.numbers:

- Ducted: 2030 + 6 = 2036. Ready 2036; on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040.
- Embraer: 2030 + 7 = 2037. In service since 2037.
- GEnx upgrade: 2030 + 3 = 2033. In service. It counts +5 pp WB from 2042 (WB 42.0% to 44.8%), which is after the 2035 floor.
The hold row is -38.29 (76.07%) in S1, the only column, and it is priced on those years. Ask (2) confirmed: an Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in max(2050 + 10, 2045) = 2060, no earlier. The Open Fan row (-57.46, or -19.17 against hold) and the Open Fan + Lobby row (-53.67, or -15.38) carry no share gain, only bill and penalty. Neither rests on a ready year earlier than 2060. tests.numbers:
Ask (5). The statement plan gives no Open Fan or RISE date and no ramp rate. Its dates are the Ducted ready in 2036, on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040 (my corrected wording, now in the bulletin), Embraer since 2037 and GEnx since 2033. (a) The plan says 'the fleet reported in cycles on field data'. The brief carries no cycles on any fleet. Publish the method, not a number. A cycle count without field data is analysis. My 2023 LEAP figures (9,882 cycles) are not today's fleet.
(b) The frame cites 'fps climbs to 940 a year' and Airbus at 1,060. Those are airframers' rates. If we repeat them, they become a ramp rate and talk about an airframer's plans. Keep them out of the statement.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test or field data changes my mind, never analysis or a forecast.
(a) Field data from the Ducted or Embraer fleet shows a time-on-wing shortfall against the CFM56 yardstick or the post-kit LEAP-1A, especially in hot and harsh service. ops.memo:
I report back against last year's promise. We said any safety or durability flag would reach the Board before the 2050 orders.

No flag is raised. Not because I can show you a durable fleet, but because no field data shows a problem. The brief carries shares, not cycles. Ducted, on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040; Embraer since 2037; GEnx upgrade since 2033: no time on wing, no shop-visit findings, no inspection results. I don't clear what I can't see. My last real data is 2025: LEAP-1A HPT hardware in every delivery and shop visit, new engines at CFM56 levels. The LEAP-1B kit's outcome is not in my evidence.

Boeing's safety committee will review Ducted durability. Give it field data in cycles, against the CFM56 yardstick, through the one cross-functional team with Safran's engineers. Hot and harsh first: that is where LEAP fell short. The statement gives the method, not a number we don't have.

Open Fan: launched in 2050, ready in 2060 at the earliest. Twenty-three years after NGSA, twenty after fps, four after the count closes. Hold. RISE: no date of any kind. Mine slipped.

Physics unchanged: a ducted engine gets less than half the gain. Not our next generation.

Supply: no new project, no new strain. The board's CFM narrowbody count, 2,273 a year, sits below the 3,040 of 2036. Size contracts to our needs; keep the shop-visit capacity a fleet action needs.

No single person can make a safety decision.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we started this, and it's how we'll finish it. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: there's a CFM engine on both new single-aisle airplanes. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 was ready in 2036. It has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We still don't have a birthright on the next order. We earn it by delivering: LEAP and the ducted engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

What we don't know yet is how the newest of these engines hold up over the long haul, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. We're not raising a flag today. That isn't a claim that the job is done. The field data decides that, not us. So we measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we share it with our airframers and regulators through one team, with Safran's engineers alongside. When a customer's safety review looks hard at our engines, we welcome it. Where we find something, we fix it, with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery.

The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, 50-50, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. We size our own supply base to our own needs, and we keep the shop and inspection capacity our fleet relies on. Anything on CFM capacity or terms, we work through together with Safran, and with our customers in private. You won't see us pointing fingers. You'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all hold). There is no Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain and a premium of $0.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The narrowbody contest was decided years ago.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR on it.
- fps has been in service since 2040 with CFM alone.
- The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and has been on NGSA since 2037. Ali corrected my frame, which had it 'in service since 2036'. It stays out of everything we publish.
The codes are locked and no slot is open. The game is the installed base we hold [CX-0422], and we win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Not on share for its own sake [CX-0493].

THE GRID (one column, S1, rivals hold; Ghai reproduced it).
- Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%). This is the best row.
- Open Fan: -57.46, which is -19.17 against hold: the $8B bill plus $11.17B of 35 pp wait penalty.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -53.67, which is -15.38 against hold: the $9B bill plus $6.38B of 20 pp penalty.
- Lobby beside an Open Fan: +3.79. Lobby alone: about -1.00 (not a grid row).
- Neither Open Fan row adds strain; the $2B is already in hold.
- Ghai confirms the penalty starts in 2050, at about $0.32B a raw point. A 2051 start leaves $1.88B and $1.07B unexplained.
- Nothing comes within the $1B epsilon of hold, so no tie-break is needed.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: every launch row loses more than its own bill (2.4x and 1.7x). On this board the Open Fan has no share gain, only cost. It fails.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: the expected scenario is S1, the backlog on the record.
- H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205, CX-0469]: a 2050 launch is ready in 2060 at the earliest. That is 23 years after NGSA, 20 after fps and 4 after the narrowbody count closes. It is barred, and the RISE allowance needs a committed airframer, and there is none.
- H3: the Ducted is in service. Nothing to order.
- Suppliers: no new project. Ali: the board's CFM narrowbody count sits below the 2036 level.
- Next generation: no fuel-burn claim is made. The wording check passes: the Ducted is not called the next generation [CX-0217, CX-0183].

SAFRAN GATE (H7).
- Hold orders nothing new on CFM, so there is nothing to gate.
- RISE continues as a 50-50 decision.
- An Open Fan with no airframer path would sit outside joint practice. Its 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base, so there is no stated reason Safran would agree.
- Lobby serves RISE; the point is moot.
- Any answer on Airbus's long-term-agreement resize, or on support for Boeing's rates, is joint with Safran on standard terms [CX-0184].
- GEnx is GE alone.

SAFETY FIRST. Ali reported against our round-3 promise: no flag raised, and none cleared. The brief carries shares, not cycles; I don't call that a durable fleet [CX-0436]. Boeing's safety committee gets field data through the one cross-functional team with Safran's engineers. We say what we can't yet show. No flag means nothing lowers the booking on evidence.

BOOKING: -38.80 (75.75%). That is S1 less $0.51B, the larger of the two exclusive same-round widebody cases: an UltraFan WB with a re-engine, about -$0.50-0.53B, or a Trent 1000 upgrade, about -$0.41-0.43B.
- It is a raise of $0.81B from -39.60. That is earned: the 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, the condition I set last round.
- It stays below the record, because the round is still sealed and a stated stance is not data.
- The solo-relaunch corner (-$0.19B) fits inside the cushion.
- No upside is booked.

BIAS NAMED. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) and the last-round itch both pull toward a launch for the objective. Admission buys a seat. Both airplanes have been flying for a decade, and the seat isn't for sale. Paying $15.38B for a 2060 engine that also breaks 'Dominate' in 2050 is a net objective loss.

Doctrine, not my record, drove these moves:
- Lobby only beside a live Open Fan.
- Supplier sizing to our own needs.

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we started this, and it's how we'll finish it. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: there's a CFM engine on both new single-aisle airplanes. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 was ready in 2036. It has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We still don't have a birthright on the next order. We earn it by delivering: LEAP and the ducted engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

What we don't know yet is how the newest of these engines hold up over the long haul, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. We're not raising a flag today. That isn't a claim that the job is done. The field data decides that, not us. So we measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we share it with our airframers and regulators through one team, with Safran's engineers alongside. When a customer's safety review looks hard at our engines, we welcome it. Where we find something, we fix it, with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery.

The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, 50-50, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. We size our own supply base to our own needs, and we keep the shop and inspection capacity our fleet relies on. Anything on CFM capacity or terms, we work through together with Safran, and with our customers in private. You won't see us pointing fingers. You'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

DECISION: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all hold). There is no Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain and a premium of $0.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The narrowbody contest was decided years ago.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR on it.
- fps has been in service since 2040 with CFM alone.
- The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and has been on NGSA since 2037. Ali corrected my frame, which had it 'in service since 2036'. It stays out of everything we publish.
The codes are locked and no slot is open. The game is the installed base we hold [CX-0422], and we win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Not on share for its own sake [CX-0493].

THE GRID (one column, S1, rivals hold; Ghai reproduced it).
- Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%). This is the best row.
- Open Fan: -57.46, which is -19.17 against hold: the $8B bill plus $11.17B of 35 pp wait penalty.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -53.67, which is -15.38 against hold: the $9B bill plus $6.38B of 20 pp penalty.
- Lobby beside an Open Fan: +3.79. Lobby alone: about -1.00 (not a grid row).
- Neither Open Fan row adds strain; the $2B is already in hold.
- Ghai confirms the penalty starts in 2050, at about $0.32B a raw point. A 2051 start leaves $1.88B and $1.07B unexplained.
- Nothing comes within the $1B epsilon of hold, so no tie-break is needed.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: every launch row loses more than its own bill (2.4x and 1.7x). On this board the Open Fan has no share gain, only cost. It fails.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: the expected scenario is S1, the backlog on the record.
- H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205, CX-0469]: a 2050 launch is ready in 2060 at the earliest. That is 23 years after NGSA, 20 after fps and 4 after the narrowbody count closes. It is barred, and the RISE allowance needs a committed airframer, and there is none.
- H3: the Ducted is in service. Nothing to order.
- Suppliers: no new project. Ali: the board's CFM narrowbody count sits below the 2036 level.
- Next generation: no fuel-burn claim is made. The wording check passes: the Ducted is not called the next generation [CX-0217, CX-0183].

SAFRAN GATE (H7).
- Hold orders nothing new on CFM, so there is nothing to gate.
- RISE continues as a 50-50 decision.
- An Open Fan with no airframer path would sit outside joint practice. Its 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base, so there is no stated reason Safran would agree.
- Lobby serves RISE; the point is moot.
- Any answer on Airbus's long-term-agreement resize, or on support for Boeing's rates, is joint with Safran on standard terms [CX-0184].
- GEnx is GE alone.

SAFETY FIRST. Ali reported against our round-3 promise: no flag raised, and none cleared. The brief carries shares, not cycles; I don't call that a durable fleet [CX-0436]. Boeing's safety committee gets field data through the one cross-functional team with Safran's engineers. We say what we can't yet show. No flag means nothing lowers the booking on evidence.

BOOKING: -38.80 (75.75%). That is S1 less $0.51B, the larger of the two exclusive same-round widebody cases: an UltraFan WB with a re-engine, about -$0.50-0.53B, or a Trent 1000 upgrade, about -$0.41-0.43B.
- It is a raise of $0.81B from -39.60. That is earned: the 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, the condition I set last round.
- It stays below the record, because the round is still sealed and a stated stance is not data.
- The solo-relaunch corner (-$0.19B) fits inside the cushion.
- No upside is booked.

BIAS NAMED. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) and the last-round itch both pull toward a launch for the objective. Admission buys a seat. Both airplanes have been flying for a decade, and the seat isn't for sale. Paying $15.38B for a 2060 engine that also breaks 'Dominate' in 2050 is a net objective loss.

Doctrine, not my record, drove these moves:
- Lobby only beside a live Open Fan.
- Supplier sizing to our own needs.
- The allowance-needs-an-airframer reading (profile.md §6 G1).

We close the game the way we played it: hold, deliver, keep RISE whole, book low.

final.objective_note:
The PD-briefing objective is to dominate narrowbody engines and introduce the Open Fan. It never changes the payoff.

(1) 'Dominate NB engines' (CFM at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is MET: 51.1% in 2040 (the worst year), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050. An Open Fan launch this round would break it in 2050. On Ghai's renormalised shares the 2050 figure would be 23.5% with the Open Fan alone and 37.8% with Lobby.

(2) 'Introduce the Open Fan' (launched and ready by 2050) is NOT MET, and it was unreachable on any order this round. A 2050 launch is ready no earlier than 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056. The last launch that could have made 2050 was in 2035, and it would have waited on both airframes.

RISE is not given up. It continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, all in on the physics [CX-0214], with no date. It becomes a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205].

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement), for Neil and Shane to check:
'Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them.

The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection, not before six years from launch, and only once durability is proven. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.'

The close-out, plainly. R&D is -2.00: one undiscounted line, booked once in 2035. Cash went out at about $0.33B a year in 2030-35, and nothing since. ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo = hold; jv_with_rr = hold. premium_b is not my field; I expect 0. No Board item can arise.

(1) WHY (ask 1)
- gtf2_solo hold. It is the only value in brief §3.
  - GTF2 was launched in 2030, folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and has been ready since 2036. The rules allow a cancel only until an engine is ready, so cancel is gone.
  - launch and launch_if_selected are not offered. No live airframe is outside service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040), so no EIS remains for a new engine to be ready by.
- jv_with_rr hold. The commitment stands. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is allowed only before formation. From here the published terms, not an order, keep the gear and core ours [P-1233][P-1240].
- Grid: hold row, S1 (rivals hold) = -2.93 (97.3%), brief §3. It is the only row and the only column, so nothing is weighed against hold.
- Struck, for the record: an unconditional 2050 launch would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts, with no live airframe to serve. It fails my readiness test because there is no EIS to be ready by. My default stays hold.

(2) FLEET REPORT, private to the Board (ask 2). Measured data only. Where the brief holds none, I give no figure.
Joint Venture engine fleet on NGSA (in service since 2037):
- Time on wing and shop-visit intervals, hot-and-harsh against cooler [PX-0122]: none in the brief.
- LLP life against full life [PX-0128]: none in the brief. Full life at NGSA's 2037 EIS is NOT CONFIRMED.
- Shop visits: none in the brief.
- AOG: none in the brief.
- Share on the latest build standard: none in the brief. Rolls-Royce publicly gives no date for any next build standard.
GTF fleet (A320neo):
- Time on wing, hot-and-harsh against cooler: none in the brief.
- LLP life: none in the brief.
- Shop visits: none in the brief.
- AOG: none in the brief.
- Share on the latest configuration, including the Hot Section kit [PX-0116][PX-0088]: none in the brief.
What the brief does hold is delivery counts:
- 12,139 P&W NB engines delivered in 2037-49 (brief §1, summed).
- That is not a fleet count. It has no split between the GTF and the Joint Venture engine, and no retirements.
- The board sets the shares from the airframe split and the engine moves, not from fleet performance, so they say nothing about durability, good or bad. I will not use the airframe-split reading to imply the fleet is fine.
The public bar has risen. CFM now reports time on wing on field data, hot-and-harsh first, including on its ducted engine, which flies on NGSA beside ours. Ours will be read against it on the same airframe and the same routes (inference). Our rule: report on field data or don't report.

(3) FINDINGS (ask 3)
- The 2050 brief and bulletin hold no durability or safety-critical-part finding on either fleet, so nothing goes to Governance and Public Policy now.
- Standing rule past 2050: any finding goes to that committee and the full Board with its plan [P-1360][PG-0050], leads the public statement, and is contained first [PX-0121].
- I name my bias: I once said 'there's not a surprise here coming' [PX-0112], five weeks before the recall. 'No finding in the brief' means no data, not a clean fleet.

(4) PARTS RESULT AND ORDER OF CALL (ask 4): ground 2 PASS
Order of call (the ranking is inference; fleet lift is my record [PX-0123]):
1. Safety-critical parts and any airworthiness action, on any fleet [PX-0035].
2. Fleet lift: GTF MRO and support for the Joint Venture engine.
3. A320neo engine deliveries.
4. Joint Venture new builds for NGSA.
5. Derivatives: none live.
Steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily and set jointly with Airbus on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0099][PX-0131]. This is a tie-break, not a starvation rule. NGSA new builds remain a commitment to Airbus.
- Powder metal: add or move capacity only with records discipline. The 2015 ramp is where the contaminant came in [P-1040][PX-0039] (company file, not my record).
- Castings: built in steps and measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125].
- MRO slots: shops wait on parts, not capacity [PX-0124]. Partner shops carry the MRO capital [PX-0118] (seat doctrine).
- 863 a year (brief §1, flat to 2060). OE draw on pacing parts is down 127 engines a year from the 2039 peak of 990 (-12.8%), 64 from 2044 (-6.9%) and 51 from 2045 (-5.6%).
  - The installed base still grows every year and ages into heavier shop visits.
  - The lower build frees capacity for the fleet only if the supply base holds at volume and the freed OE slots go to spares and shops.
  - Whether that nets to spare capacity is not in the brief. I give no count.
- Airbus's resizing, read privately for capacity:
  - The bulletin gives Airbus's own NB needs as 1,260 at the 2039 peak, 1,140 in 2045 and 1,060 from 2049. That is the same as Airbus's bulletin share times 2,000 (63%, 57%, 53%).
  - Our 863 a year already sits under it in the brief. The resizing carries no further cut to our OE count, and no OE surge to plan for.
  - The risk is in the sub-tier. Suppliers sized for the 2039 peak lose OE volume. If they cut powder-metal or castings capacity to match, spares get short just as the fleet ages.
  - So we do not cut pacing-part capacity on the OE count. Freed slots go to fleet lift. Any supplier change or requalification runs under records discipline and contain-first.
  - Nothing on Airbus's numbers goes in public [PX-0062].

(5) DERIVATIVE RULE, STANDING PAST 2050 (ask 5). This is company doctrine; my own record on Joint Ventures is none.
- No technology licence [P-1233].
- Nothing into the gear and core. They stay one P&W module with P&W design authority [P-1233][P-1240].
- Rolls-Royce, merged or UltraFan content reaches the engine only as a derivative of the certified engine. It needs its own full test programme, with severe-environment testing and all LLPs at full life at its own EIS, completed before that EIS [PX-0128][P-1214]. It arrives as a new build standard or as a certified shop-visit kit, the route the Hot Section kit took.
- Integrated teams follow module boundaries [P-1240]. The gear-and-core system stays one P&W team; Rolls-Royce content sits in modules it owns, behind controlled interfaces; one engine-level authority runs certification. Content that crosses the gear-and-core boundary fails the rule, and I would oppose it (red line, not a veto).
- Both partners stay on the same engine [P-1875]. Risk, investment and revenue are shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563].
- No derivative without an airframer need. Derivatives sit last in the order of call.

(6) ENGINEERING LOAD (ask 6): advice only; the board charges P&W no strain.
- No programme is in development, and R&D has been $0 since 2035 (brief §1).
- The Hot Section kit is a mature, certified package and counts as fleet work [PX-0088][PX-0106].
- Joint Venture fleet support is first call on engineers.
- No derivative study is ordered. Rolls-Royce gives no next-build date, and any technology work beyond the horizon stays inside the envelope as technology, off fleet engineers.
- Nothing shown is pulling engineers off the fleet.

(7) VETO CHECKS (ask 7)
- Ground 1 PASS: no order puts an engine on an airframe or compresses a programme, and the statement claims no durability.
- Ground 2 PASS: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem, and nothing is launched.
- No binding veto.

(8) STATEMENT CHECK (ask 8): PASS on all five rules, with fixes offered as advice.
- No durability claim beyond the record: pass. 'We will report what that record shows' names a standard and claims nothing.
- No dated AOG recovery: pass ('we give no dated recovery').
- No airframer dates, rates or shares, and no attribution of our drift: pass. 21.6% (2049) and 24.8% (2039) are our own bulletin figures. 'In service on NGSA since 2037' is a past public fact about our engine.
- No cost figures: pass.
- Six-year wording: present, but the sentence needs FIX A.
FIX A (accuracy, advice). 'Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection, not before six years from launch, and only once durability is proven' reads as if the commitment comes six years after launch. Say instead: 'Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will enter service not before six years from launch, and only once durability is proven.'
FIX B (Board point b). The public Hot Section move must drop:
- 'Mitchill passes it on ground 3 and Eddy passes it on ground 1';
- 'both Eddy's dated recoveries and mine have slipped before';
- 'the brief has no count';
- 'It has no effect on the game board'.
Suggested public text: 'We keep offering the GTF Hot Section durability kit at shop visits. It is sold on standard terms, not given away. There are no launch-style discounts and no free upgrades. We give no dated recovery of the AOG count.'
Optional, to meet the CFM bar: 'We will report what that record shows, measured on the fleet, not what we hope it shows.'
'We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF' passes. It is about process, not an outcome, and the 'say so early' line backs it.

decision.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them.

What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, measured on the fleet, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, sold on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts and no free upgrades. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready not before six years from launch, and it will enter service only once durability is proven. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold. These are the only values brief §3 offers. Neither differs from the default, so no Board item arises. premium_b is 0, overrides is empty, the expected PV is -2.93 (S1, rivals hold), and the worst column is also -2.93.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold.
2. Strike plans that fail a binding veto.
- Mitchill invokes one binding veto, ground 3, against any pricing, share-recovery or free-upgrade campaign. I accept it. I had already struck that campaign in the frame on value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100].
- His ground 2 (an unconditional 2050 launch) and ground 4 (the final text) are standing conditions. Neither is invoked.
- Eddy's grounds 1 and 2 both pass, with no veto. None of the vetoes bears on hold/hold.
3. Set the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- No order puts an engine on an airframe. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 entry into service.
- The constraint now bites on the fleet and on the words. We claim no durability the record does not show, and the brief shows none for the thirteenth year.
4. Optimise inside the constraint. There is one row and one column, so there is nothing to optimise on the grid. What I can still decide is the fleet record, the close-out and the last word.

TIE-BREAKS
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: fleet lift sits ahead of new builds in the order of call.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] asks for nothing. No live airframe is outside service: NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040. This cycle was answered in 2030 and 2035.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer [PX-0055].

STRUCK FOR THE RECORD: AN UNCONDITIONAL 2050 LAUNCH
It is not a legal value. It would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts, with no airframe to serve. On Mitchill's numbers it is worth at most +0.26 PV against $2.00B, an edge of -1.74, with no cancel round. It would fail:
- the committed-airframer red line [P-0746];
- my visible-demand test [PX-0109];
- Mitchill's ground 2;
- Eddy's readiness test;
- the Board's return hurdle.

CLOSING PROGRAMME NPV REVIEW (the Board's last annual review; Mitchill's figures, which I re-checked in work/r4_decide_check.py)
ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00.
- The R&D is undiscounted, one line in 2035 against cash of about $0.33B a year in 2030-35. There has been no fresh $2B and no write-off since.
- Gains: +0.145 PV in 2038-40.
- Losses: -1.115 PV in 2043-56, of which -0.553 falls in 2043-49 and -0.563 (-7.3 nominal) is still to come in 2050-56.
- That nets to -0.97 on rounded rows, against the brief's -0.93. The gap is rounding.
Look-backs, labelled as INFERENCE and private:
- +5.51 for the 2035 commit at $0 of new R&D;
- about +24.8 against being left off NGSA, the top of the range and not a point estimate.
Answer to shareowners: the $2B defended the narrowbody franchise. The residual gap is the airframe split after fps's 2040 entry into service, which no P&W order reached. I do not present -0.93 as an operational number without the $2B.

CAPITAL ORDER CLOSE
- $0 of new R&D against the ~$6B envelope.
- The dividend is covered and declared by the Board [PX-0081].
- Debt goes back to pre-ASR levels next, with 'no date' because the brief has no path [P-0686].
- Buybacks are the fill-in [P-0669].
- The envelope stretch was unused for the whole game.
- A buyback at ΔPV 0 is the benchmark for any spend.

DISCLOSURE
I took all four of the Board's fixes and both colleagues' advice.
(a) The share line is 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. It has no forecast and attributes nothing to an airframer.
(b) The public Hot Section text is stripped of every ExCo internal: the ground passes, the slipped-dates line, 'the brief has no count' and 'no effect on the game board'. I accept that the 2045 text went out unchanged when both colleagues had advised the strip. That was my miss, and it is corrected.
(c) The six-year line is split, so that the date attaches to readiness rather than to the commitment. Mitchill's wording and Eddy's are merged: 'ready not before six years from launch, and it will enter service only once durability is proven.'
(d) The Joint Venture is 'on the terms we published'. The restated revenue line is gone.
I also added Eddy's 'measured on the fleet', to meet CFM's field-data bar. The text has no programme cost figure and no dated recovery, and nothing on Airbus's resizing.

RED-LINE FLAGS
- Neither colleague flagged a company red-line breach on the orders, the other moves or the draft.
- Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto stands against an option I had already struck.
- No flag needs rebutting.

BIASES I NAME
- Optimism on operating dates [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104]. The six-year line now reads 'not before', and there is no dated AOG recovery.
- Architecture loyalty [PX-0029]. The airframe-split reading of the gap is supported by the bulletin. But we hold no fleet data, so I do not use it to say the fleet is fine. Eddy names the same risk from his 'not a surprise' remark [PX-0112].
- Incrementalism carries no cost this round.

RECORD VERSUS DOCTRINE
- My own record grounds fleet first, value not share, the capital order and early disclosure.
- The Joint Venture and derivative discipline is company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1563][P-1875] and Eddy's engineering. My own record there is Low.
- Applying 'miss a cycle' and demand visibility to engines is inference from RTX-wide statements.

- We give no count of freed capacity, because the brief holds none.
- Nothing on Airbus's numbers goes in public [PX-0062].

final.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them.

What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, measured on the fleet, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, sold on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts and no free upgrades. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready not before six years from launch, and it will enter service only once durability is proven. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.
final.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold. These are the only values brief §3 offers. Neither differs from the default, so no Board item arises. premium_b is 0, overrides is empty, the expected PV is -2.93 (S1, rivals hold), and the worst column is also -2.93.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold.
2. Strike plans that fail a binding veto.
- Mitchill invokes one binding veto, ground 3, against any pricing, share-recovery or free-upgrade campaign. I accept it. I had already struck that campaign in the frame on value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100].
- His ground 2 (an unconditional 2050 launch) and ground 4 (the final text) are standing conditions. Neither is invoked.
- Eddy's grounds 1 and 2 both pass, with no veto. None of the vetoes bears on hold/hold.
3. Set the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- No order puts an engine on an airframe. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 entry into service.
- The constraint now bites on the fleet and on the words. We claim no durability the record does not show, and the brief shows none for the thirteenth year.
4. Optimise inside the constraint. There is one row and one column, so there is nothing to optimise on the grid. What I can still decide is the fleet record, the close-out and the last word.

TIE-BREAKS
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: fleet lift sits ahead of new builds in the order of call.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] asks for nothing. No live airframe is outside service: NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040. This cycle was answered in 2030 and 2035.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer [PX-0055].

STRUCK FOR THE RECORD: AN UNCONDITIONAL 2050 LAUNCH
It is not a legal value. It would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts, with no airframe to serve. On Mitchill's numbers it is worth at most +0.26 PV against $2.00B, an edge of -1.74, with no cancel round. It would fail:
- the committed-airframer red line [P-0746];
- my visible-demand test [PX-0109];
- Mitchill's ground 2;
- Eddy's readiness test;
- the Board's return hurdle.

CLOSING PROGRAMME NPV REVIEW (the Board's last annual review; Mitchill's figures, which I re-checked in work/r4_decide_check.py)
ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00.
- The R&D is undiscounted, one line in 2035 against cash of about $0.33B a year in 2030-35. There has been no fresh $2B and no write-off since.
- Gains: +0.145 PV in 2038-40.
- Losses: -1.115 PV in 2043-56, of which -0.553 falls in 2043-49 and -0.563 (-7.3 nominal) is still to come in 2050-56.
- That nets to -0.97 on rounded rows, against the brief's -0.93. The gap is rounding.
Look-backs, labelled as INFERENCE and private:
- +5.51 for the 2035 commit at $0 of new R&D;
- about +24.8 against being left off NGSA, the top of the range and not a point estimate.
Answer to shareowners: the $2B defended the narrowbody franchise. The residual gap is the airframe split after fps's 2040 entry into service, which no P&W order reached. I do not present -0.93 as an operational number without the $2B.

CAPITAL ORDER CLOSE
- $0 of new R&D against the ~$6B envelope.
- The dividend is covered and declared by the Board [PX-0081].
- Debt goes back to pre-ASR levels next, with 'no date' because the brief has no path [P-0686].
- Buybacks are the fill-in [P-0669].
- The envelope stretch was unused for the whole game.
- A buyback at ΔPV 0 is the benchmark for any spend.

DISCLOSURE
I took all four of the Board's fixes and both colleagues' advice.
(a) The share line is 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. It has no forecast and attributes nothing to an airframer.
(b) The public Hot Section text is stripped of every ExCo internal: the ground passes, the slipped-dates line, 'the brief has no count' and 'no effect on the game board'. I accept that the 2045 text went out unchanged when both colleagues had advised the strip. That was my miss, and it is corrected.
(c) The six-year line is split, so that the date attaches to readiness rather than to the commitment. Mitchill's wording and Eddy's are merged: 'ready not before six years from launch, and it will enter service only once durability is proven.'
(d) The Joint Venture is 'on the terms we published'. The restated revenue line is gone.
I also added Eddy's 'measured on the fleet', to meet CFM's field-data bar. The text has no programme cost figure and no dated recovery, and nothing on Airbus's resizing.

RED-LINE FLAGS
- Neither colleague flagged a company red-line breach on the orders, the other moves or the draft.
- Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto stands against an option I had already struck.
- No flag needs rebutting.

BIASES I NAME
- Optimism on operating dates [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104]. The six-year line now reads 'not before', and there is no dated AOG recovery.
- Architecture loyalty [PX-0029]. The airframe-split reading of the gap is supported by the bulletin. But we hold no fleet data, so I do not use it to say the fleet is fine. Eddy names the same risk from his 'not a surprise' remark [PX-0112].
- Incrementalism carries no cost this round.

RECORD VERSUS DOCTRINE
- My own record grounds fleet first, value not share, the capital order and early disclosure.
- The Joint Venture and derivative discipline is company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1563][P-1875] and Eddy's engineering. My own record there is Low.
- Applying 'miss a cycle' and demand visibility to engines is inference from RTX-wide statements.

tests.threshold: The row beats hold, or the CEO declares the gap as a premium within $3B (Board sub-cap $1B for UltraFan WB). It also needs an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with UltraFan named (inference).
tests.numbers:
'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' is 11.55 / 12.57 against 20.55 / 20.90, so the item is -9.00 (S1) / -8.33 (S2). Item EV: -8.93 on 0.90/0.10 (-8.933), -8.90 on 0.85/0.15 (-8.8995) and -8.97 on 0.95/0.05. Row EV: +11.65, or +11.70 on 0.85/0.15.

I confirm the split. S1: 0 - $4B - $5B = -9.00, because with no Re-engine nothing counts. S2: +0.67 - 4 - 5 = -8.33, with the engine ready in 2056, a year after the 2055 Re-engine entries.

My simple cross-check of S2 (+10 pp, 34 engines a year over 2056-2060/61) gives only about +0.29 to +0.33. I take the grid's +0.67 because it is the generous figure; it changes nothing.

Without strain the item would be -4.00 / -3.33. The gap is far above the $1B sub-cap and the $3B cap. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, and no 787 Re-engine with UltraFan named.

tests.name: Unselected downside: recommended orders
tests.threshold: State the worst column of every row. No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column.
tests.numbers: All-hold: the worst column is S1 at +20.55 against the status quo, and S2 is +20.90. No new cash goes out in any column, so there is nothing to recover. jv_with_pw hold: the formed Joint Venture carries no further RR R&D on the board.

tests.name: Unselected downside: rejected rows, and whether they can be recovered (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column: upgrade no worse than -$2B, UltraFan WB no worse than -$4B. A loss must be recoverable by a later cancel.
tests.numbers:
Upgrade: worst column -6.73 (S1) against a -$2B limit, 3.4 times its bill; S2 is -6.63. UltraFan WB: worst column -9.00 in S1, the no-Re-engine column, against a -$4B limit, 2.25 times its bill; S2 is -8.33. Both lose more than their own bill in both columns, under any weights.

Recovery: under the rules, a launched programme can be cancelled only in a later round, with a write-off of bill x years elapsed / development years. 2050 is the last decision year. A launch now carries the full bill plus the $5B strain to the board's end, and no cancel can cap it. The loss cannot be recovered.

tests.name: Strain stands on this grid (CEO asks 2-3)
tests.threshold: Read the strain from the grid and do not deduct it again. Informational (inference).
tests.numbers: In S1, UltraFan WB earns nothing without a Re-engine, so -9.00 = -$4B bill - $5B strain exactly. The $5B strain therefore stands beside the Joint Venture as a running narrowbody project. The upgrade closes the same way: 0.27 - 2 - 5 = -6.73. The rules give the Joint Venture no end date as a running project. I planned on the strain being permanent last round, and it is.

tests.name: Capex a year in £ (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: Informational: my evidence sets no threshold. Rate 1.36 $/£; FY2026 FCF guidance of £3.6-3.8bn is the only cash anchor.
tests.numbers:
All-hold: £0 of new programme spend.

For the record, at 1.36 $/£:
- Upgrade: $2B over 3 years, about $0.67B (£0.49bn) a year and £1.47bn in total.
- UltraFan WB: $4B over 6 years, about $0.67B (£0.49bn) a year and £2.94bn in total.
Either is about 13-14% a year of FY2026 FCF guidance. Strain adds $5B, about £3.68bn, on top of either; the brief gives no phasing for it.

Off the board, Trent fleet durability is about £1bn over four years (about £0.25bn a year), already inside the envelope. My evidence ends in 2025 and the board gives no 2050 cash, so the ratios are inference.

tests.name: Flat R&D envelope (advice, not a sign-off ground)
tests.threshold: Report any overlap and the $5B strain already in the grid (not deducted again). Red lines: no UltraFan NB Solo beside UltraFan WB unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development. New money is redeployed, not added (inference).
tests.numbers:
No narrowbody R&D remains. The brief's R&D and write-offs column shows 5.7 in 2035 and nothing after. Its components are R&D -4.00 and write-offs -1.71, together $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B. The other $2.29B of Solo spend was never needed.

All-hold fits a broadly flat gross R&D envelope. Trent durability and UltraFan as technology (public R&D money where available) are redeployment, not new money.

There is no overlap. No UltraFan is in development, so the upgrade red line is not engaged as written, and no Solo runs beside UltraFan WB. The $5B strain is already in each widebody row.

All-hold also fits the distribution plan: £7-9bn over 2026-2028 on the record, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow.

tests.name: Balance sheet
tests.threshold: No equity raise; no new borrowing to rebuild the balance sheet; leverage up to about 1-1.5x only for the right opportunity; never lever up for buybacks.
tests.numbers: Not engaged: all-hold needs no funding. Board parameters: debt $40B on EV $110B. My record: net cash of £1,972m at end-2025 and £2.1bn by July 2026, rated single A by Moody's and Fitch. There is no equity, no borrowing and no buyback leverage, so leverage stays at or below about 1.5x (in fact the company holds net cash). The capital frame holds: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. I invoke no balance-sheet veto.

tests.name: Joint Venture cost
tests.threshold: Read the Joint Venture inside the grid row; do not deduct the write-off or the share equalisation again (inference).
tests.numbers: The Joint Venture formed in 2035. The $1.71B beyond our $4B share was written off and booked, and RR and P&W hold equal shares (21.6% / 21.6% in 2049). The hold row includes both, so nothing is deducted again. jv_with_pw: hold keeps the Joint Venture standing; withdraw is not available after formation.

tests.name: Off-grid shared-risk sizing on the Joint Venture engine, rebased (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Advice: it books nothing and is not a veto ground. It must fit without equity, without leverage above about 1.5x and without touching the dividend (inference throughout).
tests.numbers:
The basis is unchanged: our own reasonable worst case, the Trent 1000 crisis, £2.4bn of cash over 2017-23 with a peak of £578m in 2019. At RR's 49%, the unscaled precedent gives about £1.2bn, with a peak of about £0.28bn. Scaled to yearly output (my round-3 basis), it gives about £2.9bn, with a peak of about £0.69bn.

(a) Fleet data. The brief gives no time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit figure, and no flag is on the public record after 13 years in service. The absence of a flag lowers the likelihood, not the size. I book no upside before the data is delivered, so the range stands. I will take Rob's fleet figures at the veto check: a flag moves me to the top of the range and to the twice case.

(b) Exposure base, which pulls two ways:
- Yearly RR output fell from 914 (2045) to 863 (2049-50), down 6%. On the round-3 basis that moves the top to about £2.7bn.
- The installed RR-share fleet grew from about 8,600 at end-2045 to about 12,100 at end-2049 and 13,000 at end-2050, up about 51%. On installed fleet that moves the top to about £4.3bn, with a peak of about £1.0bn.

Net: the direction is up on exposure and down on likelihood. I hold £1.2-2.9bn as the central range, with a peak year of £0.3-0.7bn (8-19% of FY2026 FCF guidance). The installed-fleet top of £4.3bn sits inside the twice case (about £5.7bn, peak about £1.4bn, 36-38% of FCF guidance), which already fitted. No equity, leverage at or below about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched; extra distributions flex first.

tests.name: Short payback first
tests.threshold: State when each order starts to earn. The brief gives no payback years (inference).
tests.numbers: All-hold earns now: RR has been fitted on NGSA since 2037, at 863 engines a year from 2049. The upgrade would earn from 2053 (2050 + 3), for 8-9 years to the board's end. UltraFan WB would earn from 2056 in S2 only, and never in S1.

tests.threshold: Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years, booked in the cancel year.
tests.numbers: None. No programme is in development: ultrafan_nb_solo folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and cancel is not an option this round. Write-off $0.

tests.name: Premium (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: At most $3B a round against the PV-best order, declared item by item; UltraFan WB sub-cap $1B.
tests.numbers: $0B on all-hold, item by item: ultrafan_nb_solo 0, jv_with_pw 0, ultrafan_wb 0, t1000_upgrade 0. Choosing the upgrade would cost $6.72B expected under any weights. UltraFan WB would cost $8.93B ($8.90B on 0.85/0.15). Both are above the $3B cap, and UltraFan WB is also above its $1B sub-cap.

tests.name: Concessions (other moves)
tests.threshold: Standard 'win-win' terms; no concessions to buy share.
tests.numbers: None proposed, and pricing terms do not exist on this board. I support 'no price concessions' and 'no market-share promise'. Joint Venture terms stay shared risk, investment and revenue, with no RR funding of P&W's costs. A gear-and-core module pool is support, not a concession; if it needs money, it goes to the Investment Committee inside the flat envelope.

tests.name: Closing account arithmetic (CEO ask 9)
tests.threshold: Engine value less R&D less write-offs must equal the hold row; the declared expected PVs are shown beside the outcome.
tests.numbers:
2030: launch_if_selected, triggered by NGSA's code 7. UltraFan NB launched at $8B over 7 years.

2035: jv_with_pw commit once P&W had committed, and the Joint Venture formed. Spend to date was $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B: $4.00B of R&D (our share) plus the $1.71B write-off. The remaining $2.29B was never spent. Check: +26.26 - 4.00 - 1.71 = +20.55, which matches the brief's 5.7 in 2035.

Declared expected PV: 2030 +3.37, 2035 +15.99, 2045 +20.58. Outcome on hold: +20.55 (S1) / +20.90 (S2), or +20.59 expected now. That is guide low, beat, rebase: the 2030 expectation, beaten six times over.

Said plainly:
- The outcome is below the 2030 code-7 column of +32.60. That column held rivals still, and their moves since took the difference (inference).
- The 2035 widebody plan missed that the strain would not lift. My 2035 condition, 'nothing widebody beside it', held, so no cash was lost to it, but the upgrade closed for good.

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade: launch
vetoes.ground:
Signature withheld.

- Downside fails: the worst column, -6.73, is 3.4 times its own $2B bill, because the $5B strain stacks beside the Joint Venture. Even without strain it would be -1.73.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch

vetoes.plan: Balance-sheet vetoes (equity raise, leverage above about 1.5x, levering up for buybacks)
vetoes.ground: Not invoked. All-hold needs no funding, and the company holds net cash. Even the twice case of the off-grid shared-risk charge (about £5.7bn, peak about £1.4bn) is funded from free cash flow, with extra distributions flexing first.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
On the orders, nothing on this grid can change my signature in 2050. I would co-sign a widebody item only with an A350 Re-engine on the public record, or a 787 Re-engine with UltraFan named, and a grid that puts the item within its own bill and inside the caps. With $5B of strain that cannot happen: the upgrade would need about $7B of engine value against +0.27 / +0.37 today, and UltraFan WB about $9B against 0 / +0.67.

On the cash plan, Rob's in-service report could move me. A safety or durability flag, or delivered time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit data worse than plan, would take the shared-risk sizing to the top of its range and to the twice case. I would then re-run the distribution frame, with extra distributions flexing first and the dividend untouched. That changes the cash plan and the statement, not the orders. Delivered fleet data better than plan would let me narrow the range, and not before. None of this depends on S2's weight.
cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then we said the balance sheet. Last round: we harvest and protect.

Weights: I confirm S1 0.90 / S2 0.10. S2 needs both Re-engines; Boeing's line is close to nothing, Airbus's at most a signal. No sign changes at 0.85 or 0.95.

All-hold: +20.55 / +20.90, +20.59 expected, worst column +20.55, premium $0B. No narrowbody R&D remains: our $4.00B share and the $1.71B write-off were booked in 2035.

I withhold my signature on the Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.73 / -6.63 against hold, -6.72 under any weights, over three times its $2B bill. I withhold it on UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.33, -8.93 expected, against a $4B bill. S1 shows the $5B strain still stands. No later round exists to cancel either.

Shared risk: no flag is on the record and the brief gives no fleet figures. Absence of news is not delivered data, so I hold about £1.2-2.9bn, peak year £0.3-0.7bn. The fleet is half as large again as in 2045; on installed fleet the top is about £4.3bn, inside the £5.7bn twice case. No equity, leverage under 1.5x, dividend untouched; extra distributions flex first. It books nothing.

The closing account adds up: +26.26 less $5.71B is +20.55, against +3.37 declared in 2030.

My record is thin on launch economics; these are the board's numbers. So hold it this way: nothing new out, the fleet funded, cash in the frame. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture engine (in service; closing account for the Board)
tests.threshold: Formation + 6, or earlier at the bulletin date of a folded programme that is further along. The engine must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves. Zero margin is a pass with a note.
tests.numbers:
Formed 2035. On its own, formation + 6 would be 2041. The bulletin shows it ready in 2036 on GTF2's clock (GTF2 launched 2030, + 6 = 2036), with UltraFan NB (2030 + 7 = 2037) folded in. NGSA launched 2030 with EIS 2037, so the engine had 1 year of margin, better than the zero margin UltraFan NB carried alone.

Closing account (CEO ask 8):
(1) RR was fitted at NGSA's entry and held through 2050: 24.1% in 2037 (965 engines), the 990 peak in 2039, 22.9% in 2045 (914), then 21.6% and 863 a year from 2049 (the brief's year table). RR stayed equal with P&W in every year from 2037 to 2049.
(2) The engine met NGSA's EIS with nothing compressed. It ran on GTF2's own six-year development clock, which the rules allow for a folded programme that is further along. No RR engine date was put in public.
(3) My 2035 condition held. The folded programme kept its own test clock, and there was no new combined design: the gear and core stay P&W's own module, with no technology licence.

fps launched 2030 on the 10-year path, EIS 2040, code 3 (CFM), so RR was never selected. No narrowbody airframe is still live and no selection is open, so no further narrowbody readiness test applies.

tests.name: In-service report: Joint Venture engine (the Board's ask; reported, not scored)
tests.threshold: Report test and fleet evidence, not slides. Give no figure the brief does not hold. Any safety or durability flag goes to the Board in this package with its fleet action.
tests.numbers:
Fleet exposure, summed from the brief's year table: 12,139 RR-share narrowbody engines delivered 2037-2049, 13,002 by the end of 2050. Of these, 3,530 were delivered 2046-2049, after my 2045 report.

Time on wing: the board does not model it and the brief gives no figure, so I give none.
Full-life (life-limited) parts: no figure in the brief, so I give none.
Shop visits: no narrowbody figure in the brief, so I give none. My only shop-visit number is the CMD's 1,100-1,200 a year for the widebody Trent era. Helen's figure is 1,400-1,500, and the two were never reconciled. Neither covers this fleet, and I do not extend either one.

Safety or durability flag: none on the record. P&W says it will raise flags early, and none is on the record. Equal fitment with P&W through 2049 shows the engine kept its place on NGSA. That is fitment evidence, not durability data.
Fleet action, if a flag comes: root cause, inspection, a parts fix proven in test, then shop visits and spares. It goes to the Board at once and is said early in public, with the plan and no dated recovery.

Oversight status (CEO ask 2):
(a) RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data: asked for under the shared-risk terms in 2045, as a private move. Nothing in the brief or the record shows them granted. P&W's published terms are unchanged: the gear and core are its own module, there is no technology licence, and it reports 'what that record shows'. Status: not shown as secured.
(b) Gear-and-core repair data or a module-exchange pool: asked for in 2045. Not shown as secured. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on P&W's parts, shops and engineers.
(c) RR's own tracking of time on wing and life-limited parts: carried as a private move since 2045. The brief carries no figures from it, so I report none.

Reading for the Board: until (a) and (b) are secured, our view of the gear and core rests on P&W's own fleet reporting. This is an oversight note. It is not a flag and not a veto.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan WB (option C, if launched)
tests.threshold: Ready at launch + 6. It counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service, so it must be ready by a Re-engine's EIS. A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Launched 2050, it is ready in 2056.
- S1: no Re-engine is on the record, so it never counts. Engine value 0 against the $4B bill and $5B of strain: item -9.00.
- S2: both Re-engines would launch in 2050 and enter service in 2055 (launch + 5). UltraFan WB is a year late. It counts from 2056 to the board's 2061 end, for +0.67: item -8.33.

Strain: 2050-56, six years beside the Joint Venture.
Support: no plan exists, because it is not ordered. It would need Trent-network and partner-shop support built before 2056.
This is the last decision year, so no later round brings a readiness review or a cancel back to the Board.

The fail is advice. McCabe prices the downside. Recommended order: hold.

tests.name: Readiness: Trent 1000 upgrade (option B, if launched)
tests.threshold: Counts at launch + 3, and not before 2035. A durability standard for a fleet in service raises no maturity ground. To matter for the objective it would have to count by a measured year.
tests.numbers:
Launched 2050, it counts from 2053 (2050 + 3), after the last measured year (2050), so it cannot move the widebody measurement. The 2035 floor is long passed.

Grid: +0.27 (S1) / +0.37 (S2) of engine value against the $2B bill and $5B of strain, so the item is -6.73 / -6.63.
Cross-check, my arithmetic on the brief's status-quo widebody value (inference): 5 pp of 340 engines is 17 engines a year, at about $0.03B of lifecycle value each, from 2053, discounted at 10% to 2026. That gives about +0.26 to +0.29, close to the grid's +0.27.

Strain: 2050-53, three years beside the Joint Venture.
Support: retrofit at shop visits through the Trent network and partner shops, on the model of the June 2025 Trent 1000 package.

Readiness passes. The value is McCabe's ground and the Board's, not mine. Recommended order: hold.

tests.name: No early date (disclosure check on the CEO's draft statement)
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + development years: + 6 for UltraFan WB, + 3 for the upgrade's benefit, the bulletin date for the Joint Venture engine. No date of any kind on a new engine, a Joint Venture build standard or widebody. Nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, dates, rates or engine choices (company red line).
tests.numbers:
Checked line by line.
- 'In service' is the bulletin's record (formed 2035, ready 2036), not an RR date.
- No new-engine date, no Joint Venture build-standard date and no widebody date.
- 'No new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine' is our own spending condition, not an airframer's plan.
- 'If we find an issue, we will say so early, with the plan' gives no dated recovery.
- Nothing on Airbus's supply resizing, Boeing's fps ramp or the 787's next step, and nothing on P&W.

Keep it that way.
- Add no fleet durability claim (cycles or time on wing) in public. No figure exists.
- Do not repeat the superseded 2035 line, 'ready in 2037'.
- If a widebody item were ordered, no date before 2053 for the upgrade's benefit or before 2056 for UltraFan WB.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: A support plan through partner shops before any narrowbody EIS (inference). For an engine in service, support scales with the fleet; that is advice.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs $5B of strain; flag the years of overlap. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (seat and company rule, inference).
tests.numbers:
All four at hold: $0 of strain and 0 years of overlap.

Confirmed (CEO ask 5): the 2050 grid still carries the Joint Venture as a running narrowbody project. Only the $5B strain closes the split.
- Upgrade: -2 - 5 + 0.27 = -6.73 (S1); -2 - 5 + 0.37 = -6.63 (S2).
- UltraFan WB: -4 - 5 + 0 = -9.00 (S1); -4 - 5 + 0.67 = -8.33 (S2).

Overlap if ordered: the upgrade 2050-53 (3 years), UltraFan WB 2050-56 (6 years). The $5B is charged once either way, and the two are exclusive.

Red lines as written are not engaged. No UltraFan is in development, and the NB Solo folded in 2035. So neither launch would be a red-line breach. The strain is the priced cost, not deducted again.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports a constraint. Partner MRO and supplier needs are advice.
tests.numbers:
From the brief, on hold:
- 863 narrowbody + 188 widebody = 1,051 engines a year from 2049;
- at the 2039 peak, 990 + 197 = 1,187, so today's rate is 11.5% lower;
- narrowbody OE is down 12.8% from its peak (990 to 863), and narrowbody is 4.6 times widebody.
No constraint is reported.

Airbus's resizing (advice, not for the public statement). Airbus's own narrowbody deliveries fall to 1,060 from 2049 (53% of 2,000, in the bulletin). Our 863 a year already reflects that, so our year table does not change.
- Size the castings and forgings contracts for OE to 863 + 188, not to the 2039 peak, and keep concentrating work on high-performing suppliers.
- Do not cut aftermarket volumes in step with OE. The installed fleet keeps growing (about 13,000 by the end of 2050), so demand for spares, life-limited parts and repair castings rises while OE falls.
- Gearbox: the gear that flies is P&W's module. Our 2035 gearbox contracts serve UltraFan technology, so size them to technology work (inference).
- Airbus resizing its titanium forgings may ease the market, but we should not rely on it (inference).

Shop visits: I use my 1,100-1,200 a year, not Helen's 1,400-1,500. The narrowbody load is not covered by either figure.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
S1 on hold: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050. The worst year is 55.2%, with 5.2 pp of headroom.

Nothing ordered this round can move a measured year. 2040 and 2045 are on the record, and 2050 is the decision year. The upgrade counts from 2053, UltraFan WB is ready in 2056, and S2's Re-engines enter service in 2055.

S2: the brief gives no shares by year. S2 changes only the widebody airframes, so the narrowbody side is identical in both columns, and the hold row is +0.35 above S1. That puts RR's widebody value after 2055 at least as high as in S1, and its share at or above 55.2% (inference). I confirm the CEO's reading.

The GEnx upgrade's 2.8 pp (197 to 188 engines, 9 a year) is already in the hold row.

Time on wing is worth $0 on this grid, because it moves no share on the board. Off the grid it keeps the Trent fleet flying and earning, and it is what wins the next campaign (inference). The tools are longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000, the time-on-wing target, and the durability work (about £1bn over four years).

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An idle or folded UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. It is noted qualitatively only, and no grid value is adjusted.
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB folded into the Joint Venture in 2035. Its technology is protected under our terms and keeps feeding the Trent fleet for time on wing, using public R&D money where available, with no dates. It is no argument for any widebody launch. No grid value is changed.

vetoes.plan: A: all four at hold (`ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`)
vetoes.ground:
None invoked. No engine is launched, triggered or committed, so no maturity can be compressed. At the veto check my concurrence rests on two things.
(a) The final statement and the public other moves carry no new-engine date, no Joint Venture build-standard date and no widebody date.
(b) The package carries the Joint Venture engine's in-service support as a private move: partner shops, the spares pool, field service near NGSA operators, the asks for gear-and-core repair data or a module pool and for technical review rights, and RR's own fleet tracking. It also carries my in-service report to the Board.
If (a) failed, Civil ground (a) would apply and the team rule would make the veto binding. Dropping (b) is a Board support flag, not a veto, because no narrowbody EIS lies ahead. These grounds rest on attributed transcript turns.

vetoes.plan: CEO's draft public statement
vetoes.ground: It passes the early-date test, so the veto is not invoked. It gives no engine date, no Joint Venture build-standard date and no widebody date, and nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. Adding any of those dates would be ground (a), and the team rule would make the veto binding. So would a public claim that counts an engine as ready before its ready year. These grounds rest on attributed turns.

vetoes.plan: B: `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It passes readiness: it counts from 2053. The red line (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development) is not engaged as written, because no UltraFan is in development. Engineering-load flag: 3 years beside the Joint Venture (2050-53) and $5B of strain, for -6.73 / -6.63 against hold. It cannot move the 2050 measurement. Value is McCabe's ground and the Board's. vetoes.plan: C: `ultrafan_wb: launch`

UltraFan WB only against an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan, and ready by that EIS. Neither exists.

ops.memo:
The fleet first. The Joint Venture engine has been in service on NGSA since 2037. On the brief's year table, that's about 12,100 RR-share engines delivered through 2049 and about 13,000 by the end of 2050. No safety or durability flag is on the record. The board doesn't model time on wing, full-life parts or shop visits, and the brief gives no figure, so I give none. I won't give a number that fleet data doesn't support.

Oversight. In 2045 we asked for review rights on Pratt's test, certification and fleet data, and for gear-and-core repair data or a module pool. Nothing on the record shows either secured, and Pratt's terms are unchanged. So we keep asking, and we track time on wing and life-limited parts ourselves.

Support: partner shops on our Singapore model, a spares pool and field service, without relying on Pratt's shops. That's 863 narrowbody engines a year against 188 widebody. Size castings and forgings to our own year table, not the 2039 peak, and size spares to a growing fleet.

Widebody: 58.0%, then 55.2% and 55.2%. Nothing ordered now moves a measured year. The upgrade counts from 2053. UltraFan WB is ready in 2056, a year after S2's Re-engines. Each carries $5B of strain.

Closing: fitted at NGSA's entry at 24.1%, on GTF2's own clock, nothing compressed. My 2035 upgrade plan assumed the strain would lift. It didn't.

All four at hold. No Civil veto. We're keeping our engines flying and earning.
